dense.text: THE DANGERS OF ANALOGY ,S S The first to bring analogical reasoning to hear against the Revealed Text was fbM$+ The first person who produced these paltry analogies in the presence of the Ligh ts of God 1 was I bib* He said, "Beyond doubt fire is superior to earth: I am of fire, and he (Adam) is of dingy earth. Let us 3 then, judge by comparing the secondary with its principal: he is of darkness, 1 of radiant light." God said, " Nay, but on the contrary there shall be no re¬ lationships : asceticism and piety shall be the (sole) avenue 1 to pre-eminence This is not the heritage of the fleeting world, so that thou shnuldst gain it by des of relationship: "tis a spiritual (heritage). Kay, these things are the heritage of the prophets; the in¬ heritors of these are the spirits of the devout. The son of Ru Jahl became a true believer for ail to see; the son of Noah became one of those who lost the way. “ The child of earth (Adam) became illumined like the moon; thou art the child of fire: get thee gone with thy face black (in disgrace)!” " The wise man has made (use of) such reasonings and investi¬ gation on a cloudy day or at night for the sake of (finding) the qibla' t But with the sun and with the Ka'ba before your face, do not seek to reason and investigate in this manner. Do not pretend that you cannot see the Ka'ba, do not avert your face irom it because you have reasoned (that it is not to be seen), God knows best what is right. When you hear a pipe from the Bird of God, you commit its outward (meaning) to memory, like a lesson, And then from yourself (out of your own head) you make some analogies; you make (what is) mere fancy into a (thing of) substance (reality). The Abadl have certain mystical expressions of which the doctrines (of external religion) are ignorant. You have learned the birds" language by the sound (alone), wo you have kindled (invented) a hundred analogies and a hundred caprices. The hearts (of the saints) are wounded by you, as the invalid (was hurt by the deaf man), (while) die tleaf man became intoxicated (overjoyed) with the vain notion of success. 1 Le, the Word of God. , 3 Lrtcridly, ' L the mifirdh or nkhe {of a mraque), " which shows the direction that [he Moslem must fnc* in prayer- lS6 MATKNAWl, BOOK I The writer of the Revelation, from (hearing) the Bird's voice, supposed that he was the Bird’s equal; t The Bird flapped a wing and blinded him ; lo, it plunged him in the abyss of death and bale. " Beware 1 do not ye also 1 , (beguiled) by a reflexion or an opinion, fall from the dignities of Heaven! J4 , s Although ye are Hardt and Mariit and superior to all (the angels) on the terrace of We are they that stand in ranks, (Yet) take mercy on the wickednesses of the wicked; do not cleave to egoism and self-conceit. Beware, lest (the Divine) jealousy come from ambush and ye fall headlong to the bottom of the earth.” They both said, "O God. Thine is the command: without Thy security' (protection) where indeed is any security ?" They were saying that, but their hearts were throbbing (with desire^— 1 “How should evil come from us? Good servants (of God) are we 1 " a4M The prick of desire in the two angels did not leave (them) until it sowed the seed of self-conceit. Then they were saying, “O ye that are composed of the (four) elements (and are) unacquainted with the purity of the spiritual beings, We will draw curtains (of light) over this (terrestrial) sky, we will come to earth and set up the canopy, We will deal justice and perform worship and every night we will fly up again to Heaven, That we may become the wonder of the world, that wc may establish safety' and security on the earth." The analogy between the state of Heaven and (that of) the earth is inexact; it has a concealed difference. Explaining that one must keep one’s own ( spiritual ) slate and (mystical) intoxication hidden from the ignorant. Hearken to the tvords of the Sage (Hakim) who lived in seclusion*, " Lay thy head in the same place where thou hast drunk the wine." When the drunken man has gone astray front a tavern, he becomes the children’s laughing-stock and plaything. Whatever w'av he goes®, he is falling in the mud^ (now) on this side and (now) on that side, and every fool is laughing at him. He (goes on) like this, while the children at his heels are without knowledge of his intoxication and the taste of his wine. , |JO All mankind are children except him that is intoxicated with J Here God is adJreisinp Hirut ami Minit. 1 Literally, "the Bug* of a purdah." The poet l » meant- * Literally* 11 on every road / 3 THE DOCTRINE OF RESERVE 187 God; none is grown-up except him that h freed from sensual desire. He (God) said, "This world is a play and pastime, and ye are children' 3 ; and God speaks truth. If you have not gone forth from (taken leave of) play, you are a child: without purity of spirit how will you he fully in** telligent (tike an adult)? Know, O youth p that the lust in which men are indulging here (in this world) is like the sexual intercourse of children. What is the child's sexual intercourse? An idle phy p com¬ pared with the sexual intercourse of a Rustam and a brave champion of Islam, The wars of mankind are like children's fights—all meaning- 3435 less, pithless, and contemptible. All their fights are (fought) with w r ooden swords* all their purposes are (centred) in futility; They all are riding on a reed-cane (hobby-horse), saying, “This is our Ruriq 1 or mule that goes like DuldulV They are (really) carrying (their hobby-horses), but in their folly tfiey have raised themselves on high: they have fancied themselves to be riders carried along the road. Wait till the day w r hen those who are borne aloft by God shall pass, galloping, beyond the nine tiers (of Heaven)! 11 The spirit and the angels shall ascend to Him at the ascen- 3+4* sion of the spirit Heaven shall tremble. Like children, ye all are riding on your skim- ye have taken hold of the comer of your skirt (to serve) as a horse. From God came (the text), 11 Verily^ opinion doth not enable (you) to dispense (wtVA the Truth)*': when did the steed of opinion run (mount) to the Heavens? While preferring (in case of doubt) the stronger of the two (alternative) opinions, do not doubt whether you see the sun w r hen it is shining l At that time (when the spirit returns to God) behold your steeds 1 Ye have made a steed of your own foot. Come, recognise that your imagination and reflection and M45 sense-perception and apprehension are like the reed-cane on which children ride. The sciences of the mystics 3 bear them (aloft); the sciences of sensual men 4 are burdens to them. When knowledge strikes on the heart (is acquired through mvstical experience), it becomes a helper (ydrij; when know¬ ledge strikes on the body (is acquired through the senses), it becomes a burden (bdri). * ‘Phe animal ridden by ihe Prophet when he ascended !o Heaven. * A mule belonging to the Pmphet. * Literally, " the men of heart." * Literally p "the men nf body, 1 l88 MATHWAWI, BOOK I God hath said, "(Like an ass) laden with his hooks"-, burden¬ some is the knowledge that is not from Himself. The knowledge that is not immediately from Himself does not endure, (it is) like the tirewoman’s paint. 34ju But when you carry this burden well, the burden wul be removed and you will be given (spiritual) joy. Beware! Do not carry this burden of knowledge for the sake of selfish desire (but mortify yourself), so that you may ride on the smooth-paced steed of knowledge. So that vou may mount the smooth-paced steed of know¬ ledge, (and that) afterwards the burden may fall from your shoulder. How wilt thou be freed from selfish desires without the cup of Hu (Him), O thou who hast become content with no more of Hu than the name of Hu} From attribute and name what comes to birth? Phantasy; and that phantasy shows the way to union with Him. mjj Hast thou ever seen a subject that shows without (the exist¬ ence of) an object that is shown: unless there is the road, there can never be the ghoul (which entices travellers to stray from the road). Hast thou ever seen a name without the reality (denoted by the name)? Or hast thou plucked a rose (gul) from the (letters) gdf and lam of (the word) gull Thou hast pronounced the name: go, seek the thing named. Know that the moon is on high, not in the water of the stream. If thou wouldst pass beyond name and letter, oh, make thyself wholly purged of self, Like (polished) iron, lose the ferruginous colour; become in thy ascetic discipline (like) a mirror without rust. 34fio Make thyself pure from the attributes of self, that thou mayst behold thine own pure untarnished essence. And behold within thy heart (all) the sciences of the prophets, without book and without preceptor and master. The Prophet said, “Amongst my people are some who are one with me in nature and aspiration: Their spirits behold me by the same light by which I am beholding them,” Without the two Sahibs' and Traditions and Traditiomsts; nay, (they behold him) in the place where they drink the Water of Life. 34*3 Know the secret of "In the evening 1 was a Kurd"; read the mystcrv of “In the morning I was an Arab." And if you desire a parable of the hidden knowledge, relate the story of the Greeks and the Chinese. 1 The title is Riven 10 two works, by BukMrt and Muslim, whitH contain well-aulhctlticoted Tniditiutls of the Prophet. THE GREEK AND CHINESE ARTISTS iSg The story of the contention between the Greeks* and the Chinese m the art of painting and picturing. The Chinese said, "We are the better artists”; the Greeks said, "The (superiority in) power and excellence belongs to us. "1 will put you to the test in this matter, said the bultan, "(and sec) which of you are approved in your claim.” The Chinese and 'the Greeks began to debate: the Greeks retired from the debate. . (Then) Lite Chinese said, "Hand over to us a particular room, and (let there be) one for you (as well)." There were two rooms with door facing door; the Chinese took one, the Greeks the other. . , . , , The Chinese requested the King to give them a hundred colours: the King opened his treasury' that they might receive that (which they sought). _ . Every- morning, by (his) bounty, the colours were dispensed from the treasury to the Chinese. The Greeks said, "No tints and colours are proper for our work, (nothing is needed) except to remove the rust. They shut the door and went on burnishing: they became MW clear and pure like the sky. There is a wav from many-colouredness^to colourlessness: colour is like the clouds, and colourlessness is a moon. Whatsoever light and splendour you see in the clouds, know that it comes from the stars and the moon and the sun. When the Chinese had finished their work, they were beating drums for joy. , , , .. . . The King entered and saw the pictures there: that (sight), as he encountered it, was robbing him of his wits. After that, he came towards the Greeks: they removed the 3**0 intervening curtain. . The reflexion of those (Chinese) pictures and works (of art) struck upon these walls which had been made pure (from stain), ' All that he had seen there (in the Chinese room) seemed more beautiful here: ’twas snatching the eye from the socket. The Greeks, Q father, are the Stiffs: (they are) without (independent of) study and books and erudition, But they have burnished their breasts (and made them) pure from greed and cupidity and avarice and hatreds. That purity of the niirror is, beyond doubt, the heart which hSj receives images innumerable. , . That Moses (the perfect saint) holds in his bosom the iormless infinite form of the Unseen (reflected) from the mirror of his Although that form is not contained in Heaven, nor in the lyo MATHNAWI, BOOK I empyrean nor in the sphere of the stars, nor (in the earth which rests) on the Fish* Because (all) those are bounded and numbered—(yet is it contained in the heart): know that the mirror of the heart hath no bound. Here the understanding becomes silent or (else) it leads into error, because the heart is with Him (God), or indeed the heart is He, 3490 The reflexion of every image shines unto everlasting from the heart alone, both with plurality and without. Unto everlasting every new image that falls on it (the heart) is appearing therein without any imperfection l. They that burnish (their hearts) have escaped from (mere) scent and colour: they behold Beauty at every moment without tarrying* They have relinquished the form and husk of knowledge, they have raised the banner of the eye of certainty 1 * Thought is gone, and they have gained light: they have gained the throat (core and essence) and the sea (ultimate source) of gnosis, 3435 Death, of which all these (others) are sore afraid, this people (die perfect Sufis) are holding in derision. None gains the victory over their hearts: the hurt falls on the oyster-shell, not on the pearL Though they have let go grammar (nahw) and jurisprudence (fiqh)i yet they have taken up (instead) mystical self-effacement ( nmh crj and spiritual poverty (faqr). Ever since the forms of the Eight Paradises have shone forth, they have found the tablets of their (the Sufis') hearts receptive, (They receive) a hundred impressions from the empyrean and the starry sphere and the void: what impressions? Nay, p tis the very sight of God. Hair the Prophet, on whom he peare, asked Zayd, “How art thou to-day and in what state hast thou risen Y ** and how Zayd answered him t saying y This morning / am a true believer * O Messenger of Allah' One morning the Prophet said to Zayd, 14 How art thou this morning, O sincere Companion?" He replied , 41 (This morning I am) a faithful servant of God. pp Again he (the Prophet) said to him, 14 Where is thy token from the garden of Faith, if it has bloomed? ” He said, ** I have been athirst irt the daytime, at night I have not slept because of love and burning griefs, 1 Ij. mystical imumcn. THE VISION OF ZAYD 191 So that I passed through (and beyond) day and night, as the point of the spear passes through the shield; For beyond (the realm of contraries) nativity and continued growth are one: hundreds of thousands of years are the same as a single hour. Everlastingness and eternity are unified (yonder): the under- jjuj standing hath no wav thither by means of inquiry / 1 The Prophet said, “Where is the traveller's gift (that thou hast brought home) from this journey ? Produce it. Where is the token of sincerity (that thou hast brought) from yon fair bind?” Zayd said, “When (other) people see the sky, I behold the Empyrean with those who dweU there. The Eight Paradises and the Seven Hells are as visible to me as the idol to the idolater, I am distinguishing the people (here), one by one, like wheat from barley in the mill, So that who is for Paradise and who shall be a stranger (to js so Paradise) is as clear to me as (the difference between) snake and fish.” The day of birth for Anatolians and Ethiopians and every race (of mankind) is the Day taken faces shall become white or black*. Before this (birth), however sinful the spirit was, it w r as in the womb (of the body) and was hidden from the people. The damned are they that are damned in the mother a womb; all of them are known by the marks of God. The body, Like a mother, is big with the spirit-child: death is the pangs and throes of birth. All the spirits that have passed over (to the next life) are 3515 waiting to see in what state that proud spirit shall be bom. The Ethiopians (the damned spirits) say , 41 It belongs to us”; the Anatolians (the blessed spirits) say T “Nay, it is comely.” As soon as it is bom into the world of spirit and (Divine) grace, there is no further difference (of opinion) between die whites (the blessed) and the blacks (the damned). If it is an Ethiopian (a damned spirit), the Ethiopians carry it off; and if it is an Anatolian (a blessed spirit), the Anatolians lead it away. Until it is bom (into the next life), it is a riddle for (all) the world: few are they that know (the destiny of) the unborn. Such a one surely is seeing by the light of God, for he has the way (the means of know ing w hat is hidden) within the skin, Frincipium aquae seminis candidum est et putchrum, but the reflexion of the spirit, (whether the spirit be) Anatolian or Ethiopian, 1 The Day of fteaurreeiitm. 19? MATHNAWt, BOOK I la giving colour (glory) to those (the Anatolians) who ore most excellent in their (original) constitution , (while) it is bearing this (other) half (i*e. the Ethiopians) down to tlie lowest depth. This discourse hath no end. Hasten back, that we may not be left behind by the caravan’s file of camels. On the Day when faces shall become while or black, by whom shall reverence still be paid to Turk and Hindoo (alike)? 3j2j In the womb (of this world) Hindoo and Turk are not dis¬ tinguishable, (but) when each is bom (into the next world) he (the seer) sees that each is miserable or glorious (according to his spiritual nature), " I am seeing them all plainly, as (they shall be) on the Day of Resurrection, like (multitudes of) people, men and women. Hark, shall I tell or shall I stop my breath (keep silence)?” Mustafa (Mohammed) bit his (Zayds) lip, as though to say, "Enough!” "O Messenger of Allah, shall I tell the mystery of the Gathering (on the Day of Judgement), shall I make the Resurrection manifest in the world to-day ? Jjet me be, that I may rend the curtains asunder, Lhat my (spiritual) substance may shine forth like a sun; s That the sun may be eclipsed by me, that I may show (the difference between)' the (fruitful) date-palm and the (barren) willow. I will show forth the mystery of Resurrection, the sterling coin and the coin mixed with alloy. The people of the left 1 with their hands cut off; 1 will show forth the colour of infidelity and the colour of the (Prophet’s) folk. I will lay bare the seven rifts (sins) of hypocrisy in the light of the moon that suffers no eclipse or waning. I will display the woollen frocks of the damned, 1 will cause the drums and kettle-drums of the prophets to be heard. jjjj Hell and the Gardens (of Paradise) and the intermediate state I will bring clearly before the eyes of the infidels, I will display the pond of Kawthar heaving (with waves), which dashes water on their (the blessed ones v ) faces, (while) its sound (rings) in their ears; And those who are running athirst round Kawthar I will name one by one (and tell) who they are; Their shoulders are rubbing against my shoulder, their cries are piercing my ears. Before my eyes the people of Paradise, from free choice, clasp each other to their bosoms, 3^* Visiting one another’s high places of honour and snatching kisses from the lip® (of the houris). 1 The damned.

dense.text: THE FRIEND OF COD THE FRIEND OF COD Z23 If Adam had taken counsel in that (matter), he would not have uttered excuses in penitence, Because when one intellect is joined with another intellect, it : prevents evil action and evil speech; (Bile) when the fleshly soul is associated with another flesh I v soul, the partial (individual) intellect becomes idle and useless. When because of loneliness you fall into despair^ you become (bright as) a sun (if you go) under the shadow (protection) of the friend. Go* seek at once the friend of God: when you have done so, Cod is your friend. He who has fixed his gaze upon seclusion (and made it his object), after all "tis from the friend (of God) that he has learned that (lesson). One muse seclude one’s self from strangers, (but) not from 2$ the friend: the fur-coat is for winter, not for spring, (If) the intellect is paired with another intellect, light increases and the way becomes plain; (But if) the fleshly soul makes merry 1 with another fleshly soul, darkness increases t the way becomes hidden. The friend is thine eve* O huntsman; keep him pure from (unsoiled by) sticks and straws. Beware! Du not make a dust with thy tongue's broom* do not make a present of rubbish to thine eye. Since the true believer is a mirror for the true believer, Ins 30 face is safe from defilement 2 . The friend is a mirror for the soul in sorrow: breathe not on the face of the mirror* Q my soul 1 Lest it cover its face on account of thy breath, thou must swallow (suppress) thy breath at every moment. Art thou Jess than earth? When a plot of earth finds a friend, that is T a springtide, it finds (gains) a hundred thousand flowers. I he tree that is united with a friend* that the sweet air (of spring), blossoms from head to foot; In autumn, when it sees (meets with) a repugnant com- jj panion, it withdraws its face and head under the coverlet And says. “A bad comrade is (the means of) stirring tip trouble: since he has come, my (best) course is to sleep. Therefore 1 will sleep, l will be (like) one of the Men of the Cave (the Seven Sleepers): that prisoner of woe (that sorely distressed one) is better than Decianus.” Their time of waking was expended by (was at the disposal of) Decianus; their sleep was the capital (fundamental source) of their renown. * Literally, "becomes laughing," i.t. friendly and familiar. Is he, being entirely pure, reflect* ihy spiritual slate and show* 'her what thou really an. 224 MATHNAWf t BOOK II Sleep, when it is accompanied by wisdom* is (spiritual) wakefulness; (but) alas for the man awake who consorts with the ignorant ( 4 ■ When the crows pitch their tents on Bali man (January), the nightingales hide themselves and are mute, Because the nightingale is silent without the rose-garden: the absence of the sun kills (the nightingale's) wakefulness. O sun, thou takes t leave of this rose-garden (the earth) in order to illumine (the region) below the earth; (But) the Sun of Divine knowledge has no motion: its place of rising is naught but the spirit and the intellect; Especially the perfect Sun which is of yonder (world of Reality): day and night its action is (giving) illumination. 45 If thou art an Alexander, come to the Sun T s rising-place: after that, wheresoever thou goest, thou art possessed of goodly splendour* After that, wheresoever thou goest, 'twill become the place of sunrise: (all) the places of sunrise will be in love with thy place of sunset. Thy bat-like senses are running towards the sunset i thy pearl-scattering senses are faring towards the sunrise* I he way of (physical) sense-perception is the way of asses* O rider: have shame* O thou that art jostling (vying) with asses! Besides these five (physical) senses there are five (spiritual) senses: those (latter) are like red gold, while these (physical) senses are like copper. so In the bazaar where they (the buyers) are expert* how should they buy the copper sense like (as though it w ere) the sense of gold? The bodily sense is eating the food of darkness; the spiritual sense is feeding from a Sum _ O thou that hast borne the baggage of thy senses to the Unseen, put forth thy hand, like Moses ? from thy bosom. O thou whose attributes are (those of) the Sun of Divine knowledge, tvhile the sun in heaven is confined to a single attribute, Now thou becomest the Sun, and now the Sea; now r the mountain of Qtf, and notv the 1 Anqa. 55 In thine essence thou art neither this nor that* O thou that art greater than (all) imaginations and more than (all) more! I he Spirit is associated (endued) with knowledge and reason : what has the Spirit to do with Arabic and Turkish? Both the mun-nkhid (who asserts the transcendence of God) and the wtushtibhth (who asserts His immanence) are bewildered by thee, Q thou who* being without image (external appearance), art (appearing) in so many forms. Sometimes the muwahhad (God regarded as the only real Being)

dense.text: PROEM PROEM lx the Name of God the Merciful, the Compassionate. Listen to the reed how it telb a tale, complaining of separa¬ tions— Saying* 11 Ever since l was parted from the reed-bed * my lament hath caused man and woman to moan* I want a bosom tom bv severance* that I may unfold (to such a one) the pain of love -desire. Every one who is left far from his source wishes back the time when he was united with it* In every company I uttered my wailful notes, I consorted 5 with the unhappy and with them that rejoice. Every one became my friend from his own opinion; none sought out my secrets from within me. _\[y secret is not far from my plaint, but ear and eye lack the light (whereby it should he apprehended). Body is not veiled from soul, nor soul from body, yet none is permitted to see the soul. I This noise pf the reed is fire* it is not wind: whoso hath not this fire* may he be naught! Tis the fire of Love that is in the reed, ’tis the fervour of 10 Love that is in the wine. The reed is the comrade of every one who has been parted from a friend: its strains pierced our hearts 1 . Only to the senseless is this sense confided: the tongue hath no customer save the ear. In our woe the days (of life) have become untimely: our days 13 travel hand in hand "with burning griefs. If our days are gone, let them go f—Tis no matter. Do Thou remain, for none is holy as Thou art! Whoever is not a fish becomes sated with His water; whoever is without daily bread finds the day long. None that is raw understands the state of the ripe: therefore my words must be brief. Farewell! G son^ burst thy chains and be free! How long wilt tltou be a bondsman to 3 silver and gold? If thou pour the sea into a pitcher* how much will it hold? z* One day's store* The pitcher, the eye of the covetous, never becomes full: the oyster-shell is not filled with pearls until it is contented. Literally ,. 1 ‘ rent our veiU," 1 Literally, « (in) the bond* of." MATHNAWf, BOOK I (alone) whose garment h rent by a (mighty) love is purged of covetousness and all defect. Hail, O Love that hringest us good gain -thou that art the physician of all our ills, The remedy of ourpride and vainglory, our Plato and our Galen! 35 Through Love the earthly body soared to the skies: the mountain began to dance and became nimble. Love inspired Mount Sinai, O lover, (so that) Sinai (was made) drunken and Moses fell in a swoon. W ere I joined (o the lip of one in accord with me, l too, like the reed, would tell all that may be told; (But) whoever is parted from one who speaks his language becomes dumb, though he have a hundred songs. When the rose is gone and the garden faded, thou wilt hear no more the nightingale's story* The Beloved is all and the lover (but) a veil; the Beloved is living and the lover a dead thing. When Love hath no care for him, he is left as a bird without wings. Alas for him then l How should I have consciousness (of aught) before or be¬ hind when the light of my Beloved is not before me and behind? I^ve wills that this Word should be shown forth; if the mirror does not reflect t how is that? Dost thou know why the mirrnr (of thy soul) reflects nothing? Because the rust is not cleared from its "face. 35 O my friends, hearken to this tale: in truth it is the very marrow of our inward state. The story of the king's falling m hme mth a handmaiden and buying her. In olden time there was a king to whom belonged the power temporal and also the power spiritual. It chanced that one day he rode with his courtiers to the chase On the king's highway the king espied a handmaiden: the soul of the king was enthralled by her. Forasmuch as the bird, his soul, was fluttering in its cage, he gave money and bought the handmaiden. 4# After he had bought her and won to his desire, hv Divine destiny she sickened. A certain man had an ass but no pack-saddle: {as soon as) he got a saddle, the wolf carried away his ass. He had a pitcher, but no water could be obtained: when he found water, the pitcher broke. The king gathered the physicians together from left and right and said to them, "The life of us both is in your hands. My life is of no account, (but) she is the life of my life J am in pain and wounded: she is my remedy.

If I become occupied w ith a difficulty {difficult question) and the answer (explanation), how shall I be able to give water to the thirsty ? dense_text_dedup.text: There is none born but is created to his true nature (Islam). It is his parents who make him a Jew or a Christian or a Magian quite as beasts produce their young with their limbs perfect. Do you see anything deficient in them? Then he quoted the Qur'an., The nature made by Allah in which He has created men there is no altering of Allah's creation; that is the right religion" (ar-Rum:)

Narrated AbdurRahman ibn Awf: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Allah the Exalted has said: I am Compassionate, and this has been derived from mercy. I have derived its name from My name. If anyone joins it, I shall join him, and if anyone cuts it off, I shall cut him off

Salman Farisi reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:Verily, there are one hundred (parts of) mercy for Allah, and it is one part of this mercy by virtue of which there is mutual love between the people and ninety-nine reserved for the Day of Resurrection

dense_two_level.text: THE DANGERS OF ANALOGY ,S S The first to bring analogical reasoning to hear against the Revealed Text was fbM$+ The first person who produced these paltry analogies in the presence of the Ligh ts of God 1 was I bib* He said, "Beyond doubt fire is superior to earth: I am of fire, and he (Adam) is of dingy earth. Hast thou ever seen a name without the reality (denoted by the name)? Or hast thou plucked a rose (gul) from the (letters) gdf and lam of (the word) gull Thou hast pronounced the name: go, seek the thing named. Know that the moon is on high, not in the water of the stream. If thou wouldst pass beyond name and letter, oh, make thyself wholly purged of self, Like (polished) iron, lose the ferruginous colour; become in thy ascetic discipline (like) a mirror without rust. 34fio Make thyself pure from the attributes of self, that thou mayst behold thine own pure untarnished essence. And behold within thy heart (all) the sciences of the prophets, without book and without preceptor and master. The Prophet said, “Amongst my people are some who are one with me in nature and aspiration: Their spirits behold me by the same light by which I am beholding them,” Without the two Sahibs' and Traditions and Traditiomsts; nay, (they behold him) in the place where they drink the Water of Life. 34*3 Know the secret of "In the evening 1 was a Kurd"; read the mystcrv of “In the morning I was an Arab." And if you desire a parable of the hidden knowledge, relate the story of the Greeks and the Chinese. 1 The title is Riven 10 two works, by BukMrt and Muslim, whitH contain well-aulhctlticoted Tniditiutls of the Prophet. THE GREEK AND CHINESE ARTISTS iSg The story of the contention between the Greeks* and the Chinese m the art of painting and picturing. The Chinese said, "We are the better artists”; the Greeks said, "The (superiority in) power and excellence belongs to us. "1 will put you to the test in this matter, said the bultan, "(and sec) which of you are approved in your claim.” The Chinese and 'the Greeks began to debate: the Greeks retired from the debate. . (Then) Lite Chinese said, "Hand over to us a particular room, and (let there be) one for you (as well)." There were two rooms with door facing door; the Chinese took one, the Greeks the other. . , . , , The Chinese requested the King to give them a hundred colours: the King opened his treasury' that they might receive that (which they sought). _ . Every- morning, by (his) bounty, the colours were dispensed from the treasury to the Chinese. The Greeks said, "No tints and colours are proper for our work, (nothing is needed) except to remove the rust. They shut the door and went on burnishing: they became MW clear and pure like the sky. There is a wav from many-colouredness^to colourlessness: colour is like the clouds, and colourlessness is a moon. Whatsoever light and splendour you see in the clouds, know that it comes from the stars and the moon and the sun. When the Chinese had finished their work, they were beating drums for joy. , , , .. . . The King entered and saw the pictures there: that (sight), as he encountered it, was robbing him of his wits. After that, he came towards the Greeks: they removed the 3**0 intervening curtain. . The reflexion of those (Chinese) pictures and works (of art) struck upon these walls which had been made pure (from stain), ' All that he had seen there (in the Chinese room) seemed more beautiful here: ’twas snatching the eye from the socket. The Greeks, Q father, are the Stiffs: (they are) without (independent of) study and books and erudition, But they have burnished their breasts (and made them) pure from greed and cupidity and avarice and hatreds. That purity of the niirror is, beyond doubt, the heart which hSj receives images innumerable. , . That Moses (the perfect saint) holds in his bosom the iormless infinite form of the Unseen (reflected) from the mirror of his Although that form is not contained in Heaven, nor in the lyo MATHNAWI, BOOK I empyrean nor in the sphere of the stars, nor (in the earth which rests) on the Fish* Because (all) those are bounded and numbered—(yet is it contained in the heart): know that the mirror of the heart hath no bound. Here the understanding becomes silent or (else) it leads into error, because the heart is with Him (God), or indeed the heart is He, 3490 The reflexion of every image shines unto everlasting from the heart alone, both with plurality and without. Unto everlasting every new image that falls on it (the heart) is appearing therein without any imperfection l. They that burnish (their hearts) have escaped from (mere) scent and colour: they behold Beauty at every moment without tarrying* They have relinquished the form and husk of knowledge, they have raised the banner of the eye of certainty 1 * Thought is gone, and they have gained light: they have gained the throat (core and essence) and the sea (ultimate source) of gnosis, 3435 Death, of which all these (others) are sore afraid, this people (die perfect Sufis) are holding in derision. None gains the victory over their hearts: the hurt falls on the oyster-shell, not on the pearL Though they have let go grammar (nahw) and jurisprudence (fiqh)i yet they have taken up (instead) mystical self-effacement ( nmh crj and spiritual poverty (faqr). Ever since the forms of the Eight Paradises have shone forth, they have found the tablets of their (the Sufis') hearts receptive, (They receive) a hundred impressions from the empyrean and the starry sphere and the void: what impressions? Nay, p tis the very sight of God. Hair the Prophet, on whom he peare, asked Zayd, “How art thou to-day and in what state hast thou risen Y ** and how Zayd answered him t saying y This morning / am a true believer * O Messenger of Allah' One morning the Prophet said to Zayd, 14 How art thou this morning, O sincere Companion?" He replied , 41 (This morning I am) a faithful servant of God. pp Again he (the Prophet) said to him, 14 Where is thy token from the garden of Faith, if it has bloomed? ” He said, ** I have been athirst irt the daytime, at night I have not slept because of love and burning griefs, 1 Ij. mystical imumcn. THE VISION OF ZAYD 191 So that I passed through (and beyond) day and night, as the point of the spear passes through the shield; For beyond (the realm of contraries) nativity and continued growth are one: hundreds of thousands of years are the same as a single hour. Everlastingness and eternity are unified (yonder): the under- jjuj standing hath no wav thither by means of inquiry / 1 The Prophet said, “Where is the traveller's gift (that thou hast brought home) from this journey ? Produce it. Where is the token of sincerity (that thou hast brought) from yon fair bind?” Zayd said, “When (other) people see the sky, I behold the Empyrean with those who dweU there. The Eight Paradises and the Seven Hells are as visible to me as the idol to the idolater, I am distinguishing the people (here), one by one, like wheat from barley in the mill, So that who is for Paradise and who shall be a stranger (to js so Paradise) is as clear to me as (the difference between) snake and fish.” The day of birth for Anatolians and Ethiopians and every race (of mankind) is the Day taken faces shall become white or black*. Before this (birth), however sinful the spirit was, it w r as in the womb (of the body) and was hidden from the people. The damned are they that are damned in the mother a womb; all of them are known by the marks of God. The body, Like a mother, is big with the spirit-child: death is the pangs and throes of birth. All the spirits that have passed over (to the next life) are 3515 waiting to see in what state that proud spirit shall be bom. The Ethiopians (the damned spirits) say , 41 It belongs to us”; the Anatolians (the blessed spirits) say T “Nay, it is comely.” As soon as it is bom into the world of spirit and (Divine) grace, there is no further difference (of opinion) between die whites (the blessed) and the blacks (the damned). If it is an Ethiopian (a damned spirit), the Ethiopians carry it off; and if it is an Anatolian (a blessed spirit), the Anatolians lead it away. Until it is bom (into the next life), it is a riddle for (all) the world: few are they that know (the destiny of) the unborn. MATHNAWt, BOOK I la giving colour (glory) to those (the Anatolians) who ore most excellent in their (original) constitution , (while) it is bearing this (other) half (i*e. the Ethiopians) down to tlie lowest depth. This discourse hath no end. Hasten back, that we may not be left behind by the caravan’s file of camels. On the Day when faces shall become while or black, by whom shall reverence still be paid to Turk and Hindoo (alike)? 3j2j In the womb (of this world) Hindoo and Turk are not dis¬ tinguishable, (but) when each is bom (into the next world) he (the seer) sees that each is miserable or glorious (according to his spiritual nature), " I am seeing them all plainly, as (they shall be) on the Day of Resurrection, like (multitudes of) people, men and women. Hark, shall I tell or shall I stop my breath (keep silence)?” Mustafa (Mohammed) bit his (Zayds) lip, as though to say, "Enough!” "O Messenger of Allah, shall I tell the mystery of the Gathering (on the Day of Judgement), shall I make the Resurrection manifest in the world to-day ? Jjet me be, that I may rend the curtains asunder, Lhat my (spiritual) substance may shine forth like a sun; s That the sun may be eclipsed by me, that I may show (the difference between)' the (fruitful) date-palm and the (barren) willow. I will show forth the mystery of Resurrection, the sterling coin and the coin mixed with alloy. The people of the left 1 with their hands cut off; 1 will show forth the colour of infidelity and the colour of the (Prophet’s) folk. I will lay bare the seven rifts (sins) of hypocrisy in the light of the moon that suffers no eclipse or waning. I will display the woollen frocks of the damned, 1 will cause the drums and kettle-drums of the prophets to be heard. jjjj Hell and the Gardens (of Paradise) and the intermediate state I will bring clearly before the eyes of the infidels, I will display the pond of Kawthar heaving (with waves), which dashes water on their (the blessed ones v ) faces, (while) its sound (rings) in their ears; And those who are running athirst round Kawthar I will name one by one (and tell) who they are; Their shoulders are rubbing against my shoulder, their cries are piercing my ears. Tins wolf dealt its wound, and by way of specious excuse M came (the words) s 1 Lo+ tee went to compete with one another” Hundreds of thousands of waives have not this cunning; (but) this wolf will at last be put to shame — stop (and see)! — Because on the Day of Bale the envious will without doubt be (raised from the dead and) brought together (to Judgement) in the shape of wolves. . 1 ww* 294 MATHNAWf, BOOK IT The resurrection of the greedy vile eater of carrion (unlawful food) will be in the shape of a hog on the Day of Reckon!ng + Adulterb (erit) factor membn latentis; wine-drinkers will have stinking mouths. ms The hidden stench that was reaching (only) to (people’s) hearts will become sensible and manifest at the Resurrection. The being of Man is a jungles be on your guard against this being, if you are of that (Divine) Breath. In our being there are thousands of wolves and hogs ; (there is) goodly and ungtxnlly and fair and foul* To the disposition that is preponderant belongs the decision (as to what you are); when the gold is more than the copper* it (the mixture) is gold. I he manner of acting that preponderates in your nature- — in that same form you must needs rise (from the dead). r, * M At one hour a w F oll enters into Man, ac another hour a moon- like beauty with the face of Joseph. Good and hateful qualities pass from bosoms into bosoms by a hidden way; Nay t indeed, wisdom and knowledge and excellence pass from Man into the ox and the ass. The stumbling (restive) horse becomes smooth-paced and docile; the bear dances, the goat also salaams. Volition has passed from human beings into the dog, so that he has become a shepherd or a hunter or a guardian (of the house)* Into the dog of the Companions (of the Cave) there passed from those Sleepers a (moral) disposition, so that he had become a seeker of God* At every- moment a (different) species bursts up in the breast: now a devil, and now an ange| t now r wild beasts. h torn that iMpellous Jungle with which every lion is acquainted, there is a hidden way to the breasts which ensnare (trie spiritual prey) 1 , O you who are less than a dog, steal the spiritual pearl from within—from within (the breasts of) them that know God. As you (must) steal, at any rate (let it be) that lovely pearl; as you arc going to bear a burden, at any rate (let it be)"a noble one. How the dimples understood that Dhu 'l-Nim had not become mad f {but} had acted with intention . 1430 The friends w ent to the prison (to inquire) about the story of Dhu 1 -Nun, and expressed an opinion concerning it, Saying, 11 Perchance he does this purposely # or there is some * Literally, “ to the snare of the brtaata/' DHU *L-NTJn AND HIS FRIENDS Zq$ (deep) wisdom (in it): he is an exemplar 1 and a shining light 3 in this religion. Far, far be it from his sea-like (profound) intelligence that madness should prompt him to folly 1 God forbid, in view of the perfection of his (spiritual) attain¬ ments, that the cloud of sickness should cover his moonl He has gone into the house (and taken refuge) from the wickedness of the vulgar: he has become mad on account of the infamy of the sane. From (feeling) the disgrace of the dull body-serving intellect* mjs he has purposely gone and become mad, Saying, 4 Bind me fast and with the tail 5 of a cow smite me on head and back, and do not dispute this (matter), That from the stroke of the part (of the cow) I may gain life, as the murdered man (gained life) from the cow of Moses* O trusty ones; That I may be made happy by the stroke of a part of the cow ; (that I may) become weli (whole), like the murdered man (by means) of the cow of Moses 1 / 1 The murdered man was revived by the stroke of the cow's tail: lie became pure gold (in spirit), even as copper (is trans¬ muted) by the elixir. The murdered man sprang up and told the secrets: he revealed that bloodthirsty gang. He said plainly, “I was killed by these people who arc now disturbed (with anger) an contending against me/ When this gross body is killed, the essence that knows (spiritual) secrets is brought to life. Its spirit beholds Paradise and Hell-fire and discerns all the mysteries. ft reveals the devilish murderers, it reveals die snare of deceit and guile. To kill the cow (the fleshly soul) is the stipulation of (imposed 1415 by) the (Sufi) Path, in order that the spirit may be restored to consciousness by the stroke of her tail Kill most quickly the cow, your fleshly soul, so that the hidden spirit may become alive and conscious. Resumption of the story of Dim 7 -A wit, may God sanctify his spirit I When those persons arrived near him, he shouted, "Hey, who are ye? Take care!” They said respectfully, “We are some of thy friends: we have come hither in devotion to ask after thee, 1 Literally, 18 One to whom all turn," 5 Literally, 11 i. sij^n or evidence / 1 ’ Literally, ** instrument / 1 MATHNAWf „ BOOK II How art thou , 0 Sea of manifold intelligence? What aspersion on thy intelligence is this (alleged) madness? 1450 How should the smoke of the bath-stove attain unto the Sun? How should the "Anaa be crushed by the crow? Do not withhold (the truth) from us: explain this matter- we are lovers (of thee): do not behave to us in this fashion. One ought not to drive lovers away or dupe them by mask and false pretence. Communicate the secret, O King; do not hide 1 thy face in the cloud, Q Moon! We are loving and true and with wounded (bleeding) hearts: in the two worlds we have fixed our hearts on thee (alone). p * He began (to use) foul words and bad names recklessly : he spoke gibberish- like madmen. He jumped up and let fly stones and sticks; the whole party fled for fear of blows. He laughed loudly and tossed his head (in scorn), "Look,” said he t "at the vain bluster 3 of these friends! See the friends! Where is the sign of (true) friends? To (true) friends pain is as (dear as) life.” How should a friend turn aside from the pain inflicted bv his friend? Pain is the kernel, and friendship is fonlv) as the husk to it. r x M<kl nq * i°y ’ n tribulation and calamity- and suffering become the sign of (true) friendship? A friend is like gold, tribulation is like the fire: the pure gold is glad in the heart of the fire. Hots Lttqmdn's master tested his sagacity. (Was it) not (the case) that (this happened) to Luqman, who was a pure (unselfish) slave, and day and night was brisk in service? His master used to prefer him (to all ethers) in the work (of service) and deem him better than his own sons. Because Luqmdn, though he was slave-born, was the master (ot himself) and was free from sensual desire nsj A certain king said to the Shaykh (spiritual Director) in conversatioiij Ask me to bestow some bounty upon thee.** He answered, O King, are nol you ashamed to say such a thing to me? Come higher! J I have two slaves, and they are vile, and those two are ruler* and lords over you/ 1 Literally, "put covertly™ l Literally, "(l he IsctenO i/ and vdj.’ Literally, ihc wind of the brand.”

hybrid.text: THE DANGERS OF ANALOGY ,S S The first to bring analogical reasoning to hear against the Revealed Text was fbM$+ The first person who produced these paltry analogies in the presence of the Ligh ts of God 1 was I bib* He said, "Beyond doubt fire is superior to earth: I am of fire, and he (Adam) is of dingy earth. Let us 3 then, judge by comparing the secondary with its principal: he is of darkness, 1 of radiant light." God said, " Nay, but on the contrary there shall be no re¬ lationships : asceticism and piety shall be the (sole) avenue 1 to pre-eminence This is not the heritage of the fleeting world, so that thou shnuldst gain it by des of relationship: "tis a spiritual (heritage). Kay, these things are the heritage of the prophets; the in¬ heritors of these are the spirits of the devout. The son of Ru Jahl became a true believer for ail to see; the son of Noah became one of those who lost the way. “ The child of earth (Adam) became illumined like the moon; thou art the child of fire: get thee gone with thy face black (in disgrace)!” " The wise man has made (use of) such reasonings and investi¬ gation on a cloudy day or at night for the sake of (finding) the qibla' t But with the sun and with the Ka'ba before your face, do not seek to reason and investigate in this manner. Do not pretend that you cannot see the Ka'ba, do not avert your face irom it because you have reasoned (that it is not to be seen), God knows best what is right. When you hear a pipe from the Bird of God, you commit its outward (meaning) to memory, like a lesson, And then from yourself (out of your own head) you make some analogies; you make (what is) mere fancy into a (thing of) substance (reality). The Abadl have certain mystical expressions of which the doctrines (of external religion) are ignorant. You have learned the birds" language by the sound (alone), wo you have kindled (invented) a hundred analogies and a hundred caprices. The hearts (of the saints) are wounded by you, as the invalid (was hurt by the deaf man), (while) die tleaf man became intoxicated (overjoyed) with the vain notion of success. 1 Le, the Word of God. , 3 Lrtcridly, ' L the mifirdh or nkhe {of a mraque), " which shows the direction that [he Moslem must fnc* in prayer- lS6 MATKNAWl, BOOK I The writer of the Revelation, from (hearing) the Bird's voice, supposed that he was the Bird’s equal; t The Bird flapped a wing and blinded him ; lo, it plunged him in the abyss of death and bale. " Beware 1 do not ye also 1 , (beguiled) by a reflexion or an opinion, fall from the dignities of Heaven! J4 , s Although ye are Hardt and Mariit and superior to all (the angels) on the terrace of We are they that stand in ranks, (Yet) take mercy on the wickednesses of the wicked; do not cleave to egoism and self-conceit. Beware, lest (the Divine) jealousy come from ambush and ye fall headlong to the bottom of the earth.” They both said, "O God. Thine is the command: without Thy security' (protection) where indeed is any security ?" They were saying that, but their hearts were throbbing (with desire^— 1 “How should evil come from us? Good servants (of God) are we 1 " a4M The prick of desire in the two angels did not leave (them) until it sowed the seed of self-conceit. Then they were saying, “O ye that are composed of the (four) elements (and are) unacquainted with the purity of the spiritual beings, We will draw curtains (of light) over this (terrestrial) sky, we will come to earth and set up the canopy, We will deal justice and perform worship and every night we will fly up again to Heaven, That we may become the wonder of the world, that wc may establish safety' and security on the earth." The analogy between the state of Heaven and (that of) the earth is inexact; it has a concealed difference. Explaining that one must keep one’s own ( spiritual ) slate and (mystical) intoxication hidden from the ignorant. Hearken to the tvords of the Sage (Hakim) who lived in seclusion*, " Lay thy head in the same place where thou hast drunk the wine." When the drunken man has gone astray front a tavern, he becomes the children’s laughing-stock and plaything. Whatever w'av he goes®, he is falling in the mud^ (now) on this side and (now) on that side, and every fool is laughing at him. He (goes on) like this, while the children at his heels are without knowledge of his intoxication and the taste of his wine. , |JO All mankind are children except him that is intoxicated with J Here God is adJreisinp Hirut ami Minit. 1 Literally, "the Bug* of a purdah." The poet l » meant- * Literally* 11 on every road / 3 THE DOCTRINE OF RESERVE 187 God; none is grown-up except him that h freed from sensual desire. He (God) said, "This world is a play and pastime, and ye are children' 3 ; and God speaks truth. If you have not gone forth from (taken leave of) play, you are a child: without purity of spirit how will you he fully in** telligent (tike an adult)? Know, O youth p that the lust in which men are indulging here (in this world) is like the sexual intercourse of children. What is the child's sexual intercourse? An idle phy p com¬ pared with the sexual intercourse of a Rustam and a brave champion of Islam, The wars of mankind are like children's fights—all meaning- 3435 less, pithless, and contemptible. All their fights are (fought) with w r ooden swords* all their purposes are (centred) in futility; They all are riding on a reed-cane (hobby-horse), saying, “This is our Ruriq 1 or mule that goes like DuldulV They are (really) carrying (their hobby-horses), but in their folly tfiey have raised themselves on high: they have fancied themselves to be riders carried along the road. Wait till the day w r hen those who are borne aloft by God shall pass, galloping, beyond the nine tiers (of Heaven)! 11 The spirit and the angels shall ascend to Him at the ascen- 3+4* sion of the spirit Heaven shall tremble. Like children, ye all are riding on your skim- ye have taken hold of the comer of your skirt (to serve) as a horse. From God came (the text), 11 Verily^ opinion doth not enable (you) to dispense (wtVA the Truth)*': when did the steed of opinion run (mount) to the Heavens? While preferring (in case of doubt) the stronger of the two (alternative) opinions, do not doubt whether you see the sun w r hen it is shining l At that time (when the spirit returns to God) behold your steeds 1 Ye have made a steed of your own foot. Come, recognise that your imagination and reflection and M45 sense-perception and apprehension are like the reed-cane on which children ride. The sciences of the mystics 3 bear them (aloft); the sciences of sensual men 4 are burdens to them. When knowledge strikes on the heart (is acquired through mvstical experience), it becomes a helper (ydrij; when know¬ ledge strikes on the body (is acquired through the senses), it becomes a burden (bdri). * ‘Phe animal ridden by ihe Prophet when he ascended !o Heaven. * A mule belonging to the Pmphet. * Literally, " the men of heart." * Literally p "the men nf body, 1 l88 MATHWAWI, BOOK I God hath said, "(Like an ass) laden with his hooks"-, burden¬ some is the knowledge that is not from Himself. The knowledge that is not immediately from Himself does not endure, (it is) like the tirewoman’s paint. 34ju But when you carry this burden well, the burden wul be removed and you will be given (spiritual) joy. Beware! Do not carry this burden of knowledge for the sake of selfish desire (but mortify yourself), so that you may ride on the smooth-paced steed of knowledge. So that vou may mount the smooth-paced steed of know¬ ledge, (and that) afterwards the burden may fall from your shoulder. How wilt thou be freed from selfish desires without the cup of Hu (Him), O thou who hast become content with no more of Hu than the name of Hu} From attribute and name what comes to birth? Phantasy; and that phantasy shows the way to union with Him. mjj Hast thou ever seen a subject that shows without (the exist¬ ence of) an object that is shown: unless there is the road, there can never be the ghoul (which entices travellers to stray from the road). Hast thou ever seen a name without the reality (denoted by the name)? Or hast thou plucked a rose (gul) from the (letters) gdf and lam of (the word) gull Thou hast pronounced the name: go, seek the thing named. Know that the moon is on high, not in the water of the stream. If thou wouldst pass beyond name and letter, oh, make thyself wholly purged of self, Like (polished) iron, lose the ferruginous colour; become in thy ascetic discipline (like) a mirror without rust. 34fio Make thyself pure from the attributes of self, that thou mayst behold thine own pure untarnished essence. And behold within thy heart (all) the sciences of the prophets, without book and without preceptor and master. The Prophet said, “Amongst my people are some who are one with me in nature and aspiration: Their spirits behold me by the same light by which I am beholding them,” Without the two Sahibs' and Traditions and Traditiomsts; nay, (they behold him) in the place where they drink the Water of Life. 34*3 Know the secret of "In the evening 1 was a Kurd"; read the mystcrv of “In the morning I was an Arab." And if you desire a parable of the hidden knowledge, relate the story of the Greeks and the Chinese. 1 The title is Riven 10 two works, by BukMrt and Muslim, whitH contain well-aulhctlticoted Tniditiutls of the Prophet. THE GREEK AND CHINESE ARTISTS iSg The story of the contention between the Greeks* and the Chinese m the art of painting and picturing. The Chinese said, "We are the better artists”; the Greeks said, "The (superiority in) power and excellence belongs to us. "1 will put you to the test in this matter, said the bultan, "(and sec) which of you are approved in your claim.” The Chinese and 'the Greeks began to debate: the Greeks retired from the debate. . (Then) Lite Chinese said, "Hand over to us a particular room, and (let there be) one for you (as well)." There were two rooms with door facing door; the Chinese took one, the Greeks the other. . , . , , The Chinese requested the King to give them a hundred colours: the King opened his treasury' that they might receive that (which they sought). _ . Every- morning, by (his) bounty, the colours were dispensed from the treasury to the Chinese. The Greeks said, "No tints and colours are proper for our work, (nothing is needed) except to remove the rust. They shut the door and went on burnishing: they became MW clear and pure like the sky. There is a wav from many-colouredness^to colourlessness: colour is like the clouds, and colourlessness is a moon. Whatsoever light and splendour you see in the clouds, know that it comes from the stars and the moon and the sun. When the Chinese had finished their work, they were beating drums for joy. , , , .. . . The King entered and saw the pictures there: that (sight), as he encountered it, was robbing him of his wits. After that, he came towards the Greeks: they removed the 3**0 intervening curtain. . The reflexion of those (Chinese) pictures and works (of art) struck upon these walls which had been made pure (from stain), ' All that he had seen there (in the Chinese room) seemed more beautiful here: ’twas snatching the eye from the socket. The Greeks, Q father, are the Stiffs: (they are) without (independent of) study and books and erudition, But they have burnished their breasts (and made them) pure from greed and cupidity and avarice and hatreds. That purity of the niirror is, beyond doubt, the heart which hSj receives images innumerable. , . That Moses (the perfect saint) holds in his bosom the iormless infinite form of the Unseen (reflected) from the mirror of his Although that form is not contained in Heaven, nor in the lyo MATHNAWI, BOOK I empyrean nor in the sphere of the stars, nor (in the earth which rests) on the Fish* Because (all) those are bounded and numbered—(yet is it contained in the heart): know that the mirror of the heart hath no bound. Here the understanding becomes silent or (else) it leads into error, because the heart is with Him (God), or indeed the heart is He, 3490 The reflexion of every image shines unto everlasting from the heart alone, both with plurality and without. Unto everlasting every new image that falls on it (the heart) is appearing therein without any imperfection l. They that burnish (their hearts) have escaped from (mere) scent and colour: they behold Beauty at every moment without tarrying* They have relinquished the form and husk of knowledge, they have raised the banner of the eye of certainty 1 * Thought is gone, and they have gained light: they have gained the throat (core and essence) and the sea (ultimate source) of gnosis, 3435 Death, of which all these (others) are sore afraid, this people (die perfect Sufis) are holding in derision. None gains the victory over their hearts: the hurt falls on the oyster-shell, not on the pearL Though they have let go grammar (nahw) and jurisprudence (fiqh)i yet they have taken up (instead) mystical self-effacement ( nmh crj and spiritual poverty (faqr). Ever since the forms of the Eight Paradises have shone forth, they have found the tablets of their (the Sufis') hearts receptive, (They receive) a hundred impressions from the empyrean and the starry sphere and the void: what impressions? Nay, p tis the very sight of God. Hair the Prophet, on whom he peare, asked Zayd, “How art thou to-day and in what state hast thou risen Y ** and how Zayd answered him t saying y This morning / am a true believer * O Messenger of Allah' One morning the Prophet said to Zayd, 14 How art thou this morning, O sincere Companion?" He replied , 41 (This morning I am) a faithful servant of God. pp Again he (the Prophet) said to him, 14 Where is thy token from the garden of Faith, if it has bloomed? ” He said, ** I have been athirst irt the daytime, at night I have not slept because of love and burning griefs, 1 Ij. mystical imumcn. THE VISION OF ZAYD 191 So that I passed through (and beyond) day and night, as the point of the spear passes through the shield; For beyond (the realm of contraries) nativity and continued growth are one: hundreds of thousands of years are the same as a single hour. Everlastingness and eternity are unified (yonder): the under- jjuj standing hath no wav thither by means of inquiry / 1 The Prophet said, “Where is the traveller's gift (that thou hast brought home) from this journey ? Produce it. Where is the token of sincerity (that thou hast brought) from yon fair bind?” Zayd said, “When (other) people see the sky, I behold the Empyrean with those who dweU there. The Eight Paradises and the Seven Hells are as visible to me as the idol to the idolater, I am distinguishing the people (here), one by one, like wheat from barley in the mill, So that who is for Paradise and who shall be a stranger (to js so Paradise) is as clear to me as (the difference between) snake and fish.” The day of birth for Anatolians and Ethiopians and every race (of mankind) is the Day taken faces shall become white or black*. Before this (birth), however sinful the spirit was, it w r as in the womb (of the body) and was hidden from the people. The damned are they that are damned in the mother a womb; all of them are known by the marks of God. The body, Like a mother, is big with the spirit-child: death is the pangs and throes of birth. All the spirits that have passed over (to the next life) are 3515 waiting to see in what state that proud spirit shall be bom. The Ethiopians (the damned spirits) say , 41 It belongs to us”; the Anatolians (the blessed spirits) say T “Nay, it is comely.” As soon as it is bom into the world of spirit and (Divine) grace, there is no further difference (of opinion) between die whites (the blessed) and the blacks (the damned). If it is an Ethiopian (a damned spirit), the Ethiopians carry it off; and if it is an Anatolian (a blessed spirit), the Anatolians lead it away. Until it is bom (into the next life), it is a riddle for (all) the world: few are they that know (the destiny of) the unborn. Such a one surely is seeing by the light of God, for he has the way (the means of know ing w hat is hidden) within the skin, Frincipium aquae seminis candidum est et putchrum, but the reflexion of the spirit, (whether the spirit be) Anatolian or Ethiopian, 1 The Day of fteaurreeiitm. 19? MATHNAWt, BOOK I la giving colour (glory) to those (the Anatolians) who ore most excellent in their (original) constitution , (while) it is bearing this (other) half (i*e. the Ethiopians) down to tlie lowest depth. This discourse hath no end. Hasten back, that we may not be left behind by the caravan’s file of camels. On the Day when faces shall become while or black, by whom shall reverence still be paid to Turk and Hindoo (alike)? 3j2j In the womb (of this world) Hindoo and Turk are not dis¬ tinguishable, (but) when each is bom (into the next world) he (the seer) sees that each is miserable or glorious (according to his spiritual nature), " I am seeing them all plainly, as (they shall be) on the Day of Resurrection, like (multitudes of) people, men and women. Hark, shall I tell or shall I stop my breath (keep silence)?” Mustafa (Mohammed) bit his (Zayds) lip, as though to say, "Enough!” "O Messenger of Allah, shall I tell the mystery of the Gathering (on the Day of Judgement), shall I make the Resurrection manifest in the world to-day ? Jjet me be, that I may rend the curtains asunder, Lhat my (spiritual) substance may shine forth like a sun; s That the sun may be eclipsed by me, that I may show (the difference between)' the (fruitful) date-palm and the (barren) willow. I will show forth the mystery of Resurrection, the sterling coin and the coin mixed with alloy. The people of the left 1 with their hands cut off; 1 will show forth the colour of infidelity and the colour of the (Prophet’s) folk. I will lay bare the seven rifts (sins) of hypocrisy in the light of the moon that suffers no eclipse or waning. I will display the woollen frocks of the damned, 1 will cause the drums and kettle-drums of the prophets to be heard. jjjj Hell and the Gardens (of Paradise) and the intermediate state I will bring clearly before the eyes of the infidels, I will display the pond of Kawthar heaving (with waves), which dashes water on their (the blessed ones v ) faces, (while) its sound (rings) in their ears; And those who are running athirst round Kawthar I will name one by one (and tell) who they are; Their shoulders are rubbing against my shoulder, their cries are piercing my ears. Before my eyes the people of Paradise, from free choice, clasp each other to their bosoms, 3^* Visiting one another’s high places of honour and snatching kisses from the lip® (of the houris). 1 The damned.

hybrid.text: THE FRIEND OF COD THE FRIEND OF COD Z23 If Adam had taken counsel in that (matter), he would not have uttered excuses in penitence, Because when one intellect is joined with another intellect, it : prevents evil action and evil speech; (Bile) when the fleshly soul is associated with another flesh I v soul, the partial (individual) intellect becomes idle and useless. When because of loneliness you fall into despair^ you become (bright as) a sun (if you go) under the shadow (protection) of the friend. Go* seek at once the friend of God: when you have done so, Cod is your friend. He who has fixed his gaze upon seclusion (and made it his object), after all "tis from the friend (of God) that he has learned that (lesson). One muse seclude one’s self from strangers, (but) not from 2$ the friend: the fur-coat is for winter, not for spring, (If) the intellect is paired with another intellect, light increases and the way becomes plain; (But if) the fleshly soul makes merry 1 with another fleshly soul, darkness increases t the way becomes hidden. The friend is thine eve* O huntsman; keep him pure from (unsoiled by) sticks and straws. Beware! Du not make a dust with thy tongue's broom* do not make a present of rubbish to thine eye. Since the true believer is a mirror for the true believer, Ins 30 face is safe from defilement 2 . The friend is a mirror for the soul in sorrow: breathe not on the face of the mirror* Q my soul 1 Lest it cover its face on account of thy breath, thou must swallow (suppress) thy breath at every moment. Art thou Jess than earth? When a plot of earth finds a friend, that is T a springtide, it finds (gains) a hundred thousand flowers. I he tree that is united with a friend* that the sweet air (of spring), blossoms from head to foot; In autumn, when it sees (meets with) a repugnant com- jj panion, it withdraws its face and head under the coverlet And says. “A bad comrade is (the means of) stirring tip trouble: since he has come, my (best) course is to sleep. Therefore 1 will sleep, l will be (like) one of the Men of the Cave (the Seven Sleepers): that prisoner of woe (that sorely distressed one) is better than Decianus.” Their time of waking was expended by (was at the disposal of) Decianus; their sleep was the capital (fundamental source) of their renown. * Literally, "becomes laughing," i.t. friendly and familiar. Is he, being entirely pure, reflect* ihy spiritual slate and show* 'her what thou really an. 224 MATHNAWf t BOOK II Sleep, when it is accompanied by wisdom* is (spiritual) wakefulness; (but) alas for the man awake who consorts with the ignorant ( 4 ■ When the crows pitch their tents on Bali man (January), the nightingales hide themselves and are mute, Because the nightingale is silent without the rose-garden: the absence of the sun kills (the nightingale's) wakefulness. O sun, thou takes t leave of this rose-garden (the earth) in order to illumine (the region) below the earth; (But) the Sun of Divine knowledge has no motion: its place of rising is naught but the spirit and the intellect; Especially the perfect Sun which is of yonder (world of Reality): day and night its action is (giving) illumination. 45 If thou art an Alexander, come to the Sun T s rising-place: after that, wheresoever thou goest, thou art possessed of goodly splendour* After that, wheresoever thou goest, 'twill become the place of sunrise: (all) the places of sunrise will be in love with thy place of sunset. Thy bat-like senses are running towards the sunset i thy pearl-scattering senses are faring towards the sunrise* I he way of (physical) sense-perception is the way of asses* O rider: have shame* O thou that art jostling (vying) with asses! Besides these five (physical) senses there are five (spiritual) senses: those (latter) are like red gold, while these (physical) senses are like copper. so In the bazaar where they (the buyers) are expert* how should they buy the copper sense like (as though it w ere) the sense of gold? The bodily sense is eating the food of darkness; the spiritual sense is feeding from a Sum _ O thou that hast borne the baggage of thy senses to the Unseen, put forth thy hand, like Moses ? from thy bosom. O thou whose attributes are (those of) the Sun of Divine knowledge, tvhile the sun in heaven is confined to a single attribute, Now thou becomest the Sun, and now the Sea; now r the mountain of Qtf, and notv the 1 Anqa. 55 In thine essence thou art neither this nor that* O thou that art greater than (all) imaginations and more than (all) more! I he Spirit is associated (endued) with knowledge and reason : what has the Spirit to do with Arabic and Turkish? Both the mun-nkhid (who asserts the transcendence of God) and the wtushtibhth (who asserts His immanence) are bewildered by thee, Q thou who* being without image (external appearance), art (appearing) in so many forms. Sometimes the muwahhad (God regarded as the only real Being)

hybrid.text: PROEM PROEM lx the Name of God the Merciful, the Compassionate. Listen to the reed how it telb a tale, complaining of separa¬ tions— Saying* 11 Ever since l was parted from the reed-bed * my lament hath caused man and woman to moan* I want a bosom tom bv severance* that I may unfold (to such a one) the pain of love -desire. Every one who is left far from his source wishes back the time when he was united with it* In every company I uttered my wailful notes, I consorted 5 with the unhappy and with them that rejoice. Every one became my friend from his own opinion; none sought out my secrets from within me. _\[y secret is not far from my plaint, but ear and eye lack the light (whereby it should he apprehended). Body is not veiled from soul, nor soul from body, yet none is permitted to see the soul. I This noise pf the reed is fire* it is not wind: whoso hath not this fire* may he be naught! Tis the fire of Love that is in the reed, ’tis the fervour of 10 Love that is in the wine. The reed is the comrade of every one who has been parted from a friend: its strains pierced our hearts 1 . Who ever saw a poison and antidote like the reed? Who ever saw a sympathiser and a longing lover like the reed? The reed tells of the Way full of bbod and recounts stories of the passion of Majntin. Only to the senseless is this sense confided: the tongue hath no customer save the ear. In our woe the days (of life) have become untimely: our days 13 travel hand in hand "with burning griefs. If our days are gone, let them go f—Tis no matter. Do Thou remain, for none is holy as Thou art! Whoever is not a fish becomes sated with His water; whoever is without daily bread finds the day long. None that is raw understands the state of the ripe: therefore my words must be brief. Farewell! G son^ burst thy chains and be free! How long wilt tltou be a bondsman to 3 silver and gold? If thou pour the sea into a pitcher* how much will it hold? z* One day's store* The pitcher, the eye of the covetous, never becomes full: the oyster-shell is not filled with pearls until it is contented. Literally ,. 1 ‘ rent our veiU," 1 Literally, « (in) the bond* of." MATHNAWf, BOOK I (alone) whose garment h rent by a (mighty) love is purged of covetousness and all defect. Hail, O Love that hringest us good gain -thou that art the physician of all our ills, The remedy of ourpride and vainglory, our Plato and our Galen! 35 Through Love the earthly body soared to the skies: the mountain began to dance and became nimble. Love inspired Mount Sinai, O lover, (so that) Sinai (was made) drunken and Moses fell in a swoon. W ere I joined (o the lip of one in accord with me, l too, like the reed, would tell all that may be told; (But) whoever is parted from one who speaks his language becomes dumb, though he have a hundred songs. When the rose is gone and the garden faded, thou wilt hear no more the nightingale's story* The Beloved is all and the lover (but) a veil; the Beloved is living and the lover a dead thing. When Love hath no care for him, he is left as a bird without wings. Alas for him then l How should I have consciousness (of aught) before or be¬ hind when the light of my Beloved is not before me and behind? I^ve wills that this Word should be shown forth; if the mirror does not reflect t how is that? Dost thou know why the mirrnr (of thy soul) reflects nothing? Because the rust is not cleared from its "face. 35 O my friends, hearken to this tale: in truth it is the very marrow of our inward state. The story of the king's falling m hme mth a handmaiden and buying her. In olden time there was a king to whom belonged the power temporal and also the power spiritual. It chanced that one day he rode with his courtiers to the chase On the king's highway the king espied a handmaiden: the soul of the king was enthralled by her. Forasmuch as the bird, his soul, was fluttering in its cage, he gave money and bought the handmaiden. 4# After he had bought her and won to his desire, hv Divine destiny she sickened. A certain man had an ass but no pack-saddle: {as soon as) he got a saddle, the wolf carried away his ass. He had a pitcher, but no water could be obtained: when he found water, the pitcher broke. The king gathered the physicians together from left and right and said to them, "The life of us both is in your hands. My life is of no account, (but) she is the life of my life J am in pain and wounded: she is my remedy.
