dense_two_level.text: THE MERCHANT AND THE PARROT IIozc the parrot bade farewell to the mm hunt and flew away. The parrot gave him one or two counsels full of (spiritual) ityj savour and after that bade him the farewell of parting. The merchant said to her, u Go f God protect thee! Just now thou hast shown to me a new Wav*" Said the merchant to himself, “This is the counsel for me; I will take her Way, for this Wav is shining with light. How should my soul be meaner than the parrot? The soul ought to follow a good track like this,” The harmfulness of being honoured by the people and of becoming conspicuous. The body is cage-like - the body, amidst the cajoleries of those who come in and go out, became a thorn to the soul. This one says to him, "l will be thy confidant,” and that 1850 one says, “ Nay, 1 am thy partner.” This one says to him, "There is none in existence like thee for beauty ancl eminence and for kindness and liberality.” That one says to him, "Both the worlds are thine* all our souls are thy soul's parasites/* When he sees the people intoxicated with (desire for) him, because of arrogance he loses self-control. He does not know that the Devil has cast thousands like him into the water of the river (of destruction)* The world's flattery and hypocrisy is a sweet morsel; cat less iSg* of it (eat it not), for it is a morsel full of fire. Its fire is hidden and its taste is manifest; its smoke becomes visible in the end. Do not say* "How should I swallow that praise? He is speaking from desire (for reward): I am on his track (and see quite well what he is after)/ 1 If your bdauder should satirise you in public, your heart would burn for (many) days on account of those scorches (of vituperation). Although you know that he (only) said it in disappointment because the hopes he had of you brought him no gairi h (Vet) the effect thereof is remaining within you. The same j&fo experience happens to you in the case of praise. The effect of that too lasts fur many days and becomes a source of arrogance and deception of the soul* But it does not $how r it$df> because praise is sweet; (in the case of blame) the evil shows itself, because blame is bitter* It (blame) is like (bitter) decoctions and pills which you swallow- and for a long time you arc in disturbance and pain, MATHNAWf, BOOK I Whereas s if you eat halted (sweetmeat) p its taste is momentary: this effect, like the other, is not end urine for ever. Since it does not endure (perceptibly), it endures imper¬ ceptibly: recognise every opposite by means of its opposite. When the effect of sugar endures (remains latent), after a while it produces boils that call for the lancet. Pharaoh was made (what he was) by abundance of praises; be lowly of spirit through meekness, do not domineer. So far as you can* become a slave, do not be a monarch. Suffer blows: become like the ball, do not be the bat. Otherwise, when this elegance and beauty remains with you no more, you will be loathed by those companions. iSjt? The set of people who used to flatter you deceitfully, when they behold you will call you a devil. When they see you at their doors, they all will cry, “A dead man has risen from his grave. M (You will be) like the beardless youth whom diey address as lb Lord vt that by this hypocrisy they may make him infamous. As soon as he has grown a beard in infamy, the Devil is ashamed to search after him. The Devil approaches Man for the sake of wickedness : he does not approach you because you are worse than the Devil* So long as you were a man the Devil was running at your heels and bidding you taste (his) wine. Since you have become confirmed in devilry, the Devil is fleeing from you, O good-for-nothing! At that (former) time they clung to your skirt: when you became like this they all fled. Explanation of {the Tradition) “ Whatsoever God trills tomttA to pass" We have spoken all these words, but in preparing ourselves (for the journey before us) we are naught, naught without the favours of God. Without the favours of God and God + s elect ones, angel though he be, his page is black. iwv O God, O Thou whose bounty fulfils (every') need, it is not allowable to mention any one beside Thee. This amount of guidance Thou hast bestowed (upon us); till this (present time) Thou hast covered up many a fault of ours. Cause the drop of knowledge which Thou gavest (us) hereto¬ fore to become united with Thy seas- In my soul there is a drop - of knowledge: deliver it from sensuality and from the body's clay, Before these clays drink it up, before these winds sweep it sway. THE ALM1GHTINES5 OF GOD JOJ Although, when they sweep it away. Thou art able to take it is^s back from them and redeem it. The drop that vanished in the air or was spilled (on the earth}—when did it flee {escape} from the storehouse of Thy omnipotence? If it enter into non-existence or a hundred non-existences, it will make a foot of its head (will return in headlong haste) when * Thou cal lest it. Hundreds of thousands of opposites are killing their oppo¬ sites: Thy decree is drawing them forth again {from non- existence) * There is caravan on caravan, O Lord, (speeding) continually from non-existence towards existence. In particular, every night all thoughts and understandings become naught, plunged in the deep Sea; Again at the time of dawn those Divine ones lift up their heads from the Sea, like fishes. In autumn the myriads of boughs and leaves go in rout into the sea of Death, (While) in the garden the crow clothed in black like a mourner makes lament over the (withered) greenery. ' , Again from the Lord of the land 1 comes the edict (saying) to Non-existence, “ Give back what thou hast devoured! Give up, O blaek Death, what thou hast devoured of plants 1*05 and heating herbs and leaves and grass!" O brother, collect thy wits for an instant (and think}: from moment to moment (incessantly) there is autumn and spring within thee. Behold the garden of die heart, green and moist ami fresh, full of rosebuds and cypresses and jasmines; Boughs hidden by the multitude jof leaves, vast plain and high palace hidden bv the multitude of flowers. These words, which are from Universal Reason, are the scent of those flowers and cypresses and hvacinths. Didst thou (ever) smell the Scent of a rose where no rose was? 1 *> Didst thou (ever) see the foaming of wine where no wine was? The scent is thy guide and conducts thee on thy way: it will bring thee to Eden and Kawthar, _ The scent is a remedy for the (sightless) eye; (it is) light¬ making: the eve of Jacob was opened by a scent. The foul scent darkens the eye, the scent of Joseph succours Tllou who art not a Joseph, be a Jacob: be (familiar), like him, with weeping and sore distress. Hearken to this counsel from the hageof Ghazna \ that thou j mayst feel Freshness in thy old body: 1 Literally ; "the headman of the village." 1 Sanri- t°4 MATHNAWf* BOOK I “Disdain needs a face like the rose; when thou hast not (such a face), do not indulge in 1 ill-temper. Ugly is disdain in an uncomely face, grievous is eye-ache in an unseeing eye / 1 In the presence of Joseph do not give thyself airs and behave like a beauty: offer nothing but the supplication and sighs of Jacob. The meaning of dying (as conveyed) by the parrot was supplication (self-abasement): make thyself dead in supplication and poverty (of spirit), wo That the breath of Jesus may revive thee and make thee fair and blessed as itself* How should a rock be covered with verdure by the Spring? Become earth, that thou may at grow flowers of many a hue. Years hast thou been a heart-jagging rock: once, for the sake of experiment, be earth! The story 0/ the old harper who in the time of 1 Umar, may God be well-pleased with him , on a day when he teas starving played the harp for God's sake in the graveyard. Hast thou heard that in the time of 'Umar there was a harper, a fine and glorious minstrel? The nightingale would be made beside herself by his voice: by his beautiful voice one rapture would be turned into a hundred. His breath was an ornament to assembly and congregation, and at his song the dead would arise. (He was) like Israfil (Seraphicl), whose voice will cunningly bring the souls of the dead into their bodies. Or he was (like) an accompanist z to Israfil, for his music would make the elephant grow tvings* One day l&rAfil will make a shrill sound and will give life to him that has been rotten for a hundred years. The prophets also have (spiritual) notes within, whence there comes life beyond price to them that seek (God) P The sensual ear does not hear those notes, for the sensual ear is defiled by iniquities. The note of the peri 3 is not heard by man t for he is unable to apprehend the mysteries of the peris, Although the note of the peri too belongs to this world. The note of the heart is higher than both breaths (notes) 4 . For peri and man (alike) are prisoners: bom are (captive) in the prison of this ignorance. E LitrnillVp "do not roam found*" 1 Literally, " accompanist*. 1 F Cf_ Book [II, 1473, f M one of The Jinn. * L r. the note (voice) of min and the note of the peri. THE STORY OF THE HARPER 105 Recite Q community of Jinn (and mm) in the Siiratu P- Rahman; recognise (the meaning of) j f ye be abie to pass forth , The inward notes of the saints say, at first, il O ye particles i-)=s of Id (not = Hot-being), Take heed, lift up your heads from the Id of negation, put forth your heads from this fancy and vain imagining. 0 ye who all are rotten m (the world of) generation and cor¬ ruption, vour everlasting soul neither grew nor came to birth/' If I tell (even) a tittle of those (saintly) notes, the souls will lift up their heads from the tombs. Put thine ear close, for that (melody) is not far off, but T ri$ not permitted to convey it to thee. Hark! for the saints are the Iariffla of the (present) time: from them to the dead comes Life and freshness. At their voice the dead souls in the body's grave start up in their winding-sheets. He (that is thus awakened) says, “This voice is separate from (all other) voices: to quicken (the dead) is the work of the voice of God. We (had) died and were entirely decayed: the call of God ca me: we all arose/’ The call of God, (whether it be) veiled or unveiled, bestows that which He bestowed on Mary from fils bosom. 0 ye who are rotten with death (in your hearts) underneath 1935 the skin, return from non-existence at the voice of the Friend! Absolutely, indeed, that voice is from the King (God), though it be from the larynx of God's sen-ant. He (God) lias said to him (the saint), “I am thy tongue and eye; I am thy senses and l am thy good pleasure and thy wrath. Go, for thou art (he of whom God saith), 1 By Me he hears and by Me he sees 1 : thou art the (Divine) consciousness (itself): what is the occasion (propriety') of (saying), 'Thou art the possessor of the (Divine) consciousness'? Since thou hast become p through bewilderment, * He that belongs to God/ I am thine* for s God shall belong to him/ Sometimes 1 say to thee, “Tis thou/ sometimes, 'Tis I 1 : f-j+u whatever I say, I am the Sun illuminating (all). Wheresoever 1 shine forth from the lamp-niche of a breath (Divine word), there the difficulties of a (whole) world are resolved. The darkness which the (earthly) sun did not remove, through My breath that darkness becomes like bright morning/' To an Adam He In His own person showed the (Divine) Names; to the rest He was revealing the Names by means of Adam. Do thou receive His light either from Adam or from Himself: take the wine either from the jar or from the gourd (cup), io6 MATHNAWf, BOOK ] For this gourd is very dowdy connected with the jar: the blessed gourd is not rejoiced (by the same causes) as thou art. Mustafa (Mohammed) said, “Happy he that has seen me and he that looks at him that saw my face,” When a lamp has derived (its) light from a candle, every one that sees it (the lamp) certainly sees the candle. If transmission (of the light) occurs in this way till a hundred lamps (are lighted), the seeing of the last (lamp) hecumes a meeting with the original (light) 1 . Either take with (all) thy soul from the hindmost light — there is no difference—or from the candelabrum. t s SQ Either behold the light (of God) from the lamp of the last (saints), or behold His light from the candle of those who have gone before. Explanation of the Tradition , " Verify, your Lord hath, during the days of your time , certain breathings: oh, address your- selves to {receive} them.” The Prophet said, “In these days the breathings of God prevail : Keep ear and mind (attentive) to these (spiritual) influences, catch up such-like breathings. 1 ’' The (Divine) breathing came, beheld you, and departed: it gave life to whom It would, and departed. Another breathing has arrived. Be thou heedful, that thou mavst not miss this one too, O comrade, i,., i55 The soul of fire gained therefrom an extinguisher of (its) fire, the dead soul felt within itself a movement (of life). This is the freshness and movement of the Tubd-tree, this is not like the movements of animals. If it fait on earth and heaven, their galls will turn to water at once (they will be consumed with terror). Truly, from fear of this infinite breath (they were filled with dismay): recite (the words of the Qur’an) but they reftised to bear it (the trust offered to them). Else, how should (the words) they shrank from it have been (in the Qur’dn), unless from fear of it the heart of the mountain had become blood? 1560 Yesternight this (breath) presented itself (to me) in a different guise (but) some morsels (of food) came in and barred the way. For a morsel’s sake a Luqmdn has become (held in custody as) a pledge: ’tis the time for Luqmdn: begone, O morsel! 1 I.e. the eye tees the lisht of the lost lamp, but what realty meets the eye is ihc %h"t of the candle.

dense_two_level.text: THE LION AND THE BEASTS Thy hare-soul is feeding m the desert „ (whilst) thou art (lying) at the bottom of this well of 11 How? ■ 1 and 41 Why ? IP That lion-catcher (the hare) ran towards the beasts, crying, ** Rejoice, O people, since the announcer of joy is come. G ad news! Glad news, O company of merry-makers ! That hell-hound has gone back to Hdl. Glad news! Glad news! The enemy of your lives — his teeth os* have been tom out by the vengeance of his Creator, He who smote many heads with his daws—him too the broom of Death has swept away like rubbish," How the beasts gathered round/ the hare atui spoke in praise of Mm m Then all the wild beasts assembled s joyous and laughing gleefully in rapture and excitement. They formed a ring, he (the hare) in the midst like a candle: all die animals of the desert bowed (in homage) to him. “Art thou a heavenly angel or a peri? Xo, thou art the A^rael of fierce lions. Whatever thou art, our souls are offered in sacrifice to thee. ij*q T hou hast prevailed. Health to thy hand and arm! God turned this water into thy stream. Blessing on thy hand and arm! Explain how thou didst meditate with guile, and how thou didst guilefully wipe out that ruffian. Explain, in order that the tale may be the means of curing (our malady); explain, that it may be a salve For our souls. Explain! for in consequence of the iniquity of that tyrant our souls have myriads of wounds*” IH G SixSp” said he, **it was (by) God's aid; else, who in the ttfs world is a hare (who am I, that I should have been able to do this)? He (God) bestowed power on me and gave light to my heart; the light in my heart gave strength to hand and foot," From God come preferments (to high position), from God also come changes (w hich bring one to low estate)► God in (due) course and turn is ever displaying this (Divine) aid to doubters and seers (alike)* Take heed J Do not exult in a kingdom bestowed in turns (passing from one to another). O thou who art die bondsman of Vicissitude, do not act as though thou wert free ! (But) those for whom is prepared a kingdom beyond Viriaai- t 3 ?o tude, for them the drums (of sovereignty) are beaten beyond the Seven Planets. Beyond Vicissitude are the kings everlasting; their spirits are circling with the Cupbearer perpetually. 7& MATHN AW J f BOOK I If thou wilt renounce this drinking (of worldly pleasures) for a day or two (for thv brief lifetime), thou wilt dip thy mouth in the drink of Paradise. Commentary on (the Tradition) " IVe have returned from the lesser Jihad to the greater jfthdd" O kings, we have slain die outward enemy, (hut) there re¬ mains within (us) a worse enemy than he. To slay this (enemy) is not the work of reason and intelli¬ gence: the inward lion is not subdued by the hare. u ?3 This carnal self (nafi) is Hell, and Hell is a dragon (the fire of) which is not diminished by oceans (of water). It would drink up the Seven Seas, and still the blazing of that consumer of all creatures would not become less. Stones and stony-hearted infidels enter it, miserable and shamefaced, (But) still It is not appeased by all this food, until there comes to it from God this cal!—- “x4rt thou filled, art thou filled?" It says/*Not yet; to* here is the fire, here is the glow, here is the burning I” isto It made a mouthful of and swallowed a whole world, its belly crying aloud, "h there any more?” God/from (the realm) where place is not, sets His foot on it: then it subsides at (the command) Zfe, and it teas. Inasmuch as this self of ours is a part of Hell, and all parts have the nature of the whole, To God (alone) belongs this foot (power) to kill it: who, indeed, but God should draw its bow (vanquish it)? Only the straight arrow is put on the bow, (but) this bow (of the self) has (its) arrows bent back and crooked. iis 5 Be straight, like an arrow, and escape from the bow, for without doubt every straight (arrow) will fly from the bow (to its mark). When I turned back from the outer warfare, I set my face towards the inner warfare. We have returned from the lesser Jihad, we are engaged along with die Prophet in the greater jihad. I prqy God to grant me strength and aid and (the right of) boastingthat 1 may root up with a needle 3 this mountain of Qdf. Deem of small account the lion (champion) who breaks the ranks (of the enemy): the (true) lion is he that breaks (conquers) himself, L /_*. the success which would entitle me to beast of having conquered my il wlf/ r 1 I*, slowly and painfully. * UMAR AND THE AMBASSADOR Horn the ambassador of Rum came to the Commander of the Faithful, 1 Lmar, may God be well-pleased with him , and wit¬ nessed the gifts of grace with which 1 Umar, may God be well- pleased with him, was endowed* To ‘Umar in Medina there came through the wide desert an rjgo ambassador from the Emperor of Rum. He said, * S Q ye attendants, where b the palace of the Caliph, that I may take thither my horse and baggage?'* The folk said to him, * l He has no palace: 'Umar's (only) palace is an illumined spirit. Though he has a (great) renown from being Commander (of the Faithful), he has (no dwelling except) a hut, like the poor. O brother, how wilt thou behold his palace, when hair has grown, in the eye of thy heart ? Purge thy heart S s eye of hair and defect, and then hope to e^* behold his palace. Whoever hath a spirit purged of (sensual) desires will at once behold the Presence and the Holy Porch, When Mohammed was purged of this fire and smoke (of human passions), wheresoever lie turned his face, tvas the Face of Allah. Inasmuch as thou art a friend to the evil suggestions of the malign one (Satan), how wilt thou know (the true meaning of) There is the Face of Allah} Every one in whose breast the gate is opened will behold from every city the sun (shining), God is manifest amongst others as the moon amidst the stars, u™ Lay two finger-ends on thy two eyes, and wilt thou see aught of the world? Deal justly (confess that thou wilt sec nothing). If thou dost not see this world, (yet) it is not non-existent: the fault tics not save in the huger of thy evil self. Come* lift the finger from thine eye, and then behold what¬ soever thou wishest. To Noah his people said, 1 Where is the Divine recompense? * He said, 'On the other side of they cover themselves with their garments „ Ye have wrapped your faces and heads in your clothes: of mg* necessity ye have eyes and see not,' Man is eye, and (all) the rest is (worthless) skin: the sight of that (eye) is (consists in) seeing the Beloved. When there is not sight of the Beloved, it (the eye) is better blind; the beloved who b not everlasting is better afar (away and out of sight),” When the ambassador of Rfint admitted these fresh (spiritual) words into his hearing (gave ear to them), be became more full of longing. MATHNAWf, BOOK I He fixed his eye on seeking ‘Umar, he let hi$ baggage and horse be lost. 1410 He was going in every direction after that man of (great) accomplishment, inquiring madly for him, Saying, “Can there be in the world such a man, and he be hid, like the spirit, from the world? ” He sought him, that he might be as a slave to him: inevitably the seeker is a finder. An Arab woman of the desert saw that he was a stranger- guest. “Look,” said she, “there is ‘Umar under that palm. There he is under the palm-tree, apart from the people: behold the Shadow of God asleep in the shade!*' How the ambassador of Rum found the Commander of the Faithful, * Umar, may God be toell-pleased faith him, sleeping tinder the palm-tree. 1413 He came thither and stood afar off; he saw ‘Umar and fell a-trembling. An awe came upon the ambassador from that slumbering man; a sweet ecstasy lodged in his soul. Love and awe are contrary to each other; he saw these two contraries united in his heart 1 . He said to himself : “ I have seen (many) kings, I have been great (in esteem) and chosen (for honour) in the presence of sultans: I had no awe or dread of kings, (but) awe of this man has robbed me of my wits, t4 «■ I have gone into a jungle of lions and leopards, and my face did not change colour because of them; Often where the ranks are arrayed on the field of battle have I become (fierce) as a lion at the time when the affair is grievous (desperate) ; Many a heavy blow have I suffered and inflicted, I have been stouter in heart than (all) the others. This man is asleep on the earth, unarmed, (and yet) I am trembling in my seven limbs (my whole body): what is this? This is awe of God, it is not from created beings, it is not awe of this man who wears the frock of a dervish. i^ij Whoever is afraid of God and has chosen fear of God (as his religion), the jinn and mankind and every one who sees (him) are afraid of him.” Thus meditating, he folded his hands reverently. After a while 'Umar sprang up from sleep. 1 Literally , 11 liver.' 4 UMAR AND THE AMBASSADOR How the ambassador of Rum saluted the Commander of the Faithful t may God be ell-pleased with him. He did homage to "Umar and salaamed: the Prophet said* "(First) the salaam T then the talk,” Then he (‘Umar) said, "To thee (greeting)/* called him (to come) forward, reassured him p and bade him sit down by his side + Fear ye not is die hospitality offered to those who fear: that is proper (entertainment) for one who is afraid. When any one is afraid„ they make him (feel) secure; they 1430 soothe (his) fearful heart. How should you say "Fear not" to one who has no fear? Why give lessons (to him)? He needs no lessons. lie ( A Umar) made that disturbed mind (be) of good cheer and made his desolate heart (be) flourishing (happy). Afterwards he addressed to him subtle discourses and (spoke) of the holy attributes of God — how good a Friend is He! — - And of the lovingkindnesses of God to the Abddl (saints)* in order that he (the ambassador) might know (the meaning of) magdm (permanent station) and hdl (passing state). The hdl is like the unveiling of that beauteous bride* while 143s the maqdm is the (king's) being alone with the bride. The unveiling is witnessed by the king and by others as well* (but) at the time of being alone (with the bride) there is no one except the mighty king. The bride unveils before commons and nobles (alike); in the bridal chamber the king is (alone) with the bride. There is many a one of the Sufis who enjoys hdl, (but) he that has attained to maqdm is rare amongst them. He ('Umar) reminded him of the stages traversed by the suul s and he reminded him of the journeys of the spirit. And of the Time which has (ever) been void of time, and of i-uo the Station of Holiness which has (ever) been majestical* And of the atmosphere wherein the Simurgh of the spirit h before this (material life), has flown and experienced (the bounty of Divine) grace 1 . Every single flight thereof (being) greater than the horizons (of this world) and greater than the hope and greed of the longing lover. When 'Umar found the stranger in appearance a friend (in reality), he found (that) his soul (was) seeking (to learn) the (Divine) mysteries. The Shaykh ( A Umar) was adept and the disciple (the am¬ bassador) eager: the man (rider) was quick (dexterous) and the beast belonged to the royal court (was nobly bred and docile). 1 Literally K "hits seen flight and (Divine) bounty. 9 " So MATHNAWf, BOOK I M45 That spiritual guide ('Umar) perceived that he (the am¬ bassador) possessed (the capacity for receiving) guidance: he sowed the good seed in the good soil Hose the ambassador of R um questioned the Commander of the Faithful f may God he well-phased with him m The man said to him, "'Q Commander of the Faithful* how did the spirit come to the earth from above? How did the infinite bird go into the cage?” He replied, “ Cod recited spells and incantations over the spirit* When He recites spells over the non-existences which have no eye or ear, they begin to stir. Because of His spells the non-existences at that very moment are dancing joyously into existence, ijjoi When, again. He recited a spell over the existent, at His word the existent marched (back) post-haste into non-existence. He spake into the ear of the rose and made it laughing (blooming); He spake to the stone and made it a cornelian of the mine T He spake to the body a sign (message), so that it became spirit; He spake to the sun, so that it became radiant* Again He puts into its ear a fearful saying, and upon the face of the sun fall a hundred eclipses. Consider what that Speaker chanted into the ear of the cloud, so that it poured tears from its eye, like a waterskin. 1455 Consider what God has chanted into the ear of the earth, so that it became regardful and has (ever since) remained silent/ 1 Whosoever in perplexity is sorely troubled, God has spoken the riddle into his ear, That He may imprison him in two (doubtful) thoughts, (namely), “Shall I do what He told (me) or the contrary thereof ? n From (the decree of) God also, one side obtains the prepon¬ derance, and from that (Divine) quarter he chooses one of the two (alternatives)* If thou wouldst not have the mind of thy spirit in (a state of) perplexity, do not stuff this cotton-wool into thy spiritual ear, 1460 So that thou mayst understand those riddles of His, so that thou mayst apprehend (both) the secret sign and the open. Then the spiritual car becomes the place where wahy (in¬ spiration) descends. What is wafiyl A speech hidden from sense-perception. The spiritual ear and eye are other than diis sense-perception, the ear of (discursive) reason and the car of opinion are destitute of this (inspiration). The word “compulsion” (jabr) made me impatient (uncon- 'UMAR AND THE AMBASSADOR Si tmllable) for love's sake, while it confined in (the prison of) compulsion him who is not a lover, 1 his is union with God* and it is not compulsion: this is the shining forth of the moon, this is not a cloud* And if this be compulsion, it is not the compulsion of (suffered 1465 by) the vulgar: it is not the compulsion of (exerted by) the evil- commanding self-willed (soul), Q son, (only) they know (the real meaning of) compulsion in whose hearts God has opened the sight (of the spiritual eye). 1 0 them the unseen things of the tutu re became manifest; to them recollection of the past became naught. Their freewill and compulsion is different (from that of ordinary' men): in oyster-shells drops (of rain) are pearls. Outside (01 the shell) it is a drop of water* small or great, (but) within the shell it is a small or big pearl. Those persons have the nature of the muskdeer's gland: u?a externally they are (as) blood, while within them is the fragrance of musk. Do not say* “ This substance externally is blood: how should it become a musky perfume when it goes into the gland? 1 ' Do not say s "This copper externally was despicable: bow should it assume nobility in the heart (midst) of the elixir? " In thee (the matter ol) freewill and compulsion was a (mere) fancy,(but)when it went into them it became the light of (Divine) Majesty. When bread is (wrapped) in the tablecloth it is the inanimate thing (so-called), (but) in the human body it becomes the glad spirit (of life). ' B It does nut become transmuted in the heart of (within) the table- cloth: the (animal) soul transmutes it w ith (the water of) SalsabiL G thou who reddest aright, such is the power of the soul: what, then, must he the power of that Soul of soul? The piece oi flesh which is Man, endowed with intelligence and soul p cleaves mountain and sea and mine. 1 he strength ol the mountain-riving soul b (shown in) the splitting of rocks; the strength of the Soul of sou) in the moon was split asunder. If the heart should open the lid of the wallet of (this) mystery, the soul would rush (in rapture) towards the highest heaven. Hour Adam imputed tint! fault {which he had committed) to himself^ saying , 44 O Lord, we have done wrong, ' and how IbUs imputed his own sin to God, saying, i4 Because Thou hast seduced me." Consider both our action and the action of God. Regard our i+s* action as existent. This is manifest. If the action of created beings be not in the midst (obviously existent), then say not to any one, 11 Why have you acted thus? 11 S3! G ft Sz M ATHNAWf | BOOK I The creative act of God brings our actions into existence: our actions are the effects of the creative act of God* A rational being perceives either the letter (the outer sign) or the (inner) purple (the spirit): how should he comprehend two accidents at once? If he goes (turns his mind) to the spirit, he becomes un- heedful of the letter: no eye sees forward and backward at the same moment, ■ Is5 At the time when you look in front, how at the same time can you look behind you? Recognise this. Inasmuch as the soul does not comprehend (both) the letter and the spirit, how should the soul be the creator of them both? O son, (only) God comprehends both: the (one) action does not hinder Him from the other action, Satan said Because Thou hast seduced me: the vile Devil con¬ cealed his own act. Adam said We heme done wrong unto ourselves: he was not, like us* unheedful of the action of God, if£o From respect he concealed it (the action of God) in ^regard to) the sin: by casting the sin upon himself he ate fruit (was blessed). After his repentance, ITe (God) said to him, m O Adam, did not 1 create in thee that sin and (those) tribulations? Was it not My foreordain ment and destiny? How didst thou conceal that at the time of excusing thyself? ” He (Adam) said, “I was afraid, (so) 1 did not let respect go (did not fail to observe due respect)." He (God) said* 14 1 too have observed it towards thee, 11 Whoever brings reverence gets reverence (in return): whoever brings sugar eats almond-cake. 1495 For whom are the good women ? For the good men. Treat thy friend with honour; offend (him) and see (what will happen). O heart, bring (forward) a parable for the sake of (illustrating) a difference, that thou mayst know (what distinguishes) com¬ pulsion from freewill. (Take the case of) a hand that is shaking from (morbid or involuntary) tremor and (the case of) a person whose hand you cause to shake (by knocking it away) from its place. Know that both (these) movements are created by God, but it is impossible to compare the latter with the former. You are sorry for having caused it (his hand) to shake: how r is the man afflicted with (a morbid) tremor not sorry? 1500 This is the intellectual quest. What is (the use of such a) quest, O ingenious one? 1 hat perchance (by its means) a man of weak understanding may find his way to that place (gain some idea of the truth). ‘UMAR AND THE AMBASSADOR 83 (\ fct) the intellectual quest, though it be (fine as) pearls and 13 t ™ e ^ than the spiritual quest. J he spiritual quest is on another plane; the spiritual wine has another consistency. At the time when the intellectual quest was in keeping (with the circumstances), this ‘Umar was intimate with Bu ’ 1 -Hakam, (But) when L mar went away from intellect towards spirit, Bu l-llikiim became Bu Jalil (the lather of ignorance) in searching into that (subject). ' He is perfect on the side of sense-perception and under- ijoi standing, though indeed he is ignorant in regard to the spirit. Know that the quest of the intellect and the senses is (con¬ cerned with) effects or secondary causes. The spiritual quest is either wonder or the father of wonder (either wonderful or beyond wonder). 'lire illumination of the spirit comes: (then) there remains not, O thou who seekest illumination, conclusion and premise or that which contradicts (a statement) (or) that which renders (its acceptance) necessary, Because the seer on whom His (God's) Light is dawning is qinte independent of the (logical) proof which resembles a (blind man s) staff. Commentary on “And He is with you wheresoever ye be.” Once more wc come back to the tale: when, indeed, did we go forth from the tale? If we come to ignorance, that is His prison, and if we come lSlo to knowledge, that is His palace; And it wc come to sleep, we are His intoxicated ones: and if to wakefulness, we arc in His hands; And if w r e weep, we arc a cloud laden with the bounty dis¬ pensed by Him; and if wc laugh, at that time we are His lightning 1 And if (we come) to wrath and war, 'tis the reflexion of His Might; and if to peace and forgiveness, tis the reflexion of His Love. Who are we? In this tangled (complex) world what (tiling other than He) indeed hath He (who is single) like alif> Nothing, nothing, * Uaic the ambassador asked ‘ Lmar, may God be well-pleased with him, concerning the cause of the tribulation suffered by spirits in these bodies of clay. He said, “O “Umar, what was the wisdom and mystery of ,j,j imprisoning that pure one (the spirit) in this dirty' place? The pure water has become hidden in mud: the pure spirit has become bound in bodies/* MATHNAWf,BOOK I He (*Umar) said, "Thou art making a profound inquiry, thou art confining a meaning in a word. Thou hast imprisoned the free (unconditioned) meaning, thou hast bound the wind in a word. This thou hast done for a benefit (good purpose). To speak in parables, God's jealousy is the wheat, (while) men's jealousy is die straw in the stack/ Know that the root of (all) jealousies is in God: those of mankind are an offshoot from God, without resemblance (being implied)* I will leave the explanation of this and will begin to complain of the cruelty of that fickle Beauty. I wail because wailings are pleasant to Him: He wants from the two worlds wailing and grief. How should I not wail bitterly on account of His de- 1 773 ceit, since I am not in the circle of those intoxicated with Him? How* should I not mourn, like night, without His day and without the favour of His day-illuming countenance? His unsweetness is sweet in my soul: may my soul be sacri¬ ficed to the Beloved who grieves my heart! I am in love with my grief and pain for the sake of pleasing my peerless King, I make the dust of sorrow a salve for mine eye, that the two seas of mine eyes may be filled with pearls. The tears which people shed for His sake are pearls—and people think they are tears, I am complaining of the Soul of the soul, (but in truth) I am not complaining: I am (only) relating. My heart h saying, 11 1 a m tormented by Him,” and I have (long) been laughing at its poor pretence. Du (me) right, O glory of the righteous, Q Thou who art the dais, and I the threshold of Thy door! Where are threshold and dais in reality? In the quarter where our Beloved is, where are “we” and "I”? O Thou whose soul is free from +l w r c TT and 11 1O Thou who 17S5 art the subtle essence of the spirit in man and woman, * 98 MATHNAWf, BOOK I When man and woman become one, Thuti art that One; when the units are wiped out, lo, Thou art that (Unity)* Thou didst contrive this M l a * and "we” in order that Ihou mightst play the game 1 of worship with Thyself, That all “IV T and “thou! 1 *” should become one soul and at last should he submerged in the Beloved. All this is (true)p and do Thou come, O (Lord of the) Creative Word-, O Thou who transcendest 44 Come” and (all) speech! 1 77 a The body can sec Thee (only) in bodily fashion: it fancies (pictures to itself) Thy sadness or laughter. Do not say that the heart that is bound (conditioned) by (such bodily attributes as) sadness and laughter is worthy of seeing Thee (as Thou really art). tie who is bound by sadness and laughter is living by means of these two borrowed (transient and unreal) things. In the verdant garden of Love, which is without end* there are many fruits besides sorrow and joy. Love is higher than these two states of feeling: without spring and without autumn it is (ever) green and fresh. 1735 Pay the tithe on Thy fair face* O Beauteous One: relate the story of the soul that is rent in pieces, For by the coquetry of a glance One who is given to glancing amorously has branded mv heart anew. I absolved Him if He shed my blood: I was saying, 11 It is lawful (I absolve Thee)*” and lie was fleeing (from me). Since Thou art fleeing from the lament of those who are (as) dust p why pourest Thou sorrow on the hearts of the sorrowful ? O Thou* whom every dawn that shone from the East found overflowing (with abundant grace) like the bright fountain (ol the sun}* , igoo Ilow didst Thou give (nothing but) evasion to 1 hy irenzied loverp 0 Thou the sugar of whose lips hath no price? 0 Thou who art a new soul to the old world, hear the cry (that comes) from my body (which is) without soul and heart. Leave the tale of the R "se! For God's sake set forth the tale of the Nightingale that is parted from the Rose! Our emotion is not caused by grief and joy* our consciousness is not related to fancy and imagination. There is another state (of consciousness)* which is rare: do not thou disbelieve, for God te very mighty . is*3 Do not judge from the (normal) state of man h do not abide in wrong-doing and in well-doing- Wrong-doing and well-doing, grief and joy* are things that 1 Lite rally, mrd, b kind of backgammon. * Literally, "Tht Command (which is) 'Bcf = 4, 0 Thou who E ihe Command/ 1 Another reading is THE MERCHANT AND THE PARROT 99 -cornu Into existence; those who come into existence die: God is their heir. Tis dawn. Q Thou who art the support and refuge of the dawn, ask pardon (fur me) of my Lord IlusAmu’ddm! Thou art He who asketh pardon of the Universal Mind and Soul,Thou art the Soul of the soul and the Splendour of the coral. The light of dawn has shone forth, and from Thy light we arc engaged in drinking the morning-drink with the wine of Thy Mansur L Inasmuch as Thy gift keeps me thus f crura vished), who (what) 1S10 is (other) wine that it should bring me rapture? Wine in ferment is a beggar suing for our ferment ; Heaven in revolution is a beggar suing fur our consciousness. Wine became intoxicated with us ? not we with it; the body came into being from u$, not we from it. We are as bees, and bodies are as wax (honeycomb): we have made the body, cell by cell, like wax. Revirting to the tale of the merchant who went to trade (m India). This (discourse) is very long. Tell the story of the merchant, that we may see what happened to that good man. The merchant in fire (burning grief) and anguish and yearning iSi S was uttering a hundred distracted phrases like this. Now self-contradiction, now disdain, now supplication, now passion for reality p now metaphor (unreality). The drowning man suffers an agony of soul and clutches at every straw. For fear of (losing) hi$ head (life), he flings about (both) hand and foot to see whether any one will take his hand (help him) in peril. The Friend loves this agitation: it is better to struggle vainly than to lie still. lie who is the King (of all) is not idle, (though) complaint from Him would be a marvel, fur He is not ilk For this reason said the Merciful (God), O son, 11 Every day He h [busy) in an affair” O son* In this Way be thou ever scraping and scratching (exerting thyself to the utmost): until thy last breath do not be unoccupied for a moment. So that thy last breath may be a last breath in which the (Divine) favour is thy bosom-friend. Whatsoever the soul which is in man and woman strives to do, the ear and eye of the soul's King are at the window, 1 //, Haltiij, who •said "Ana " JQQ MATHNAWJ f BOOK I How the merchant east the parrot out of the tag* and how the dead parrot flew away. i£as After that, he cost her out of the cage. The little parrot flew to a lofty bough. The dead parrot made such a (swift) flight as when the orient sun rushed onward. The merchant was amazed at the action of the bird: without understanding he suddenly beheld the mysteries of the bird. He lifted up his face and said, “O nightingale, give us profit (instruction) by explaining thy case. What did she (the parrot) do there (in India), that thou didst leam, devise a trick, and bum us (with grief) ,p ? ifiio The parrot said t “She by her act counselled me — 'Abandon thy charm of voice and thy affection (for thy master). Because thy voice has brought thee into bondage': she feigned herself dead for the sake of (giving me) this counsel. Meaning (to sayk 'O thou who hast become a singer to high and low, become dead like me, that thou mays! gain release. 111 If you are a grain, the little birds will peck you up- if you are a bud, the children will pluck you off. Hide the grain (bait), become wholly a snare j hide the bud, become the grass on the roof. 1035 Any one who offers his beauty to auction, a hundred evil fates set out towards him (and overtake him). Plots and angers and envies pour upon his head, like water from waterskins. Foes tear him to pieces from jealousy; even friends take his lifetime away. He that was heedless of the sowing and the springtide, how should he know the value of this lifetime? You must flee to the shelter of God's grace, who shed thousandfold grace upon (our) spirits, iM That you may find a shelter. Then how (will you lack) shelter? Water and fire will become your army. Did not the sea become a friend to Noah and Moses? Did it not become overbearing in vengeance against their enemies? Was not the fire a tor tress for Abraham, so that it raised smoke (sighs of despair) from the heart of Nimrod? Did not the mountain call Yahya (John the Baptist) to itself and drive off his pursuers with blows of stone? 4:1 0 Yahya,” it said," come, take refuge in me, that 1 may be thy shelter from the sharp sword/"

MUTE ELOQUENCE 411 Lies muster round (those who are living) lies: (the text) the tricked teamen far the tricked men has thrown light (upon this point). They whose hearts arc (opened) Wide (to receive spiritual .43 truths) have wide (far-reaching) hands 1 ; they whose (spiritual) eyes are blind have to stumble on stony ground. On seeking the tree whereof nane that eats the fruit shall die, A learned man (once) said, for the sake of (telling) a story, <l In India there is a certain tree: Whoso takes and eats 2 of its Fruit* he grows not old nor ever dies,” A king heard this (tale) from a veracious person; he became a lover of the tree and its fruit. From the Divan of culture he sent an intelligent envoy to India jn search (of it). For (many) years his envoy wandered about India in quest 3<H3 (of the tree). He roamed from towm to town for this object: neither island nor mountain nor plain was left (unvisited). Every- one whom he asked made a mock of him* saying* 111 Who would search after this, unless perhaps a madman in confinement?” Many slapped him jocosely; many said* “O fortunate man p How should the enquiry' of a clever and dear-minded person like you be devoid {of result)? How should it be vain?” And this (ironical) respect was to him another slap, and it .'>jq was harder (to bear) than the visible slap. They extolled him sarcastically, saying* i+ Q great sir* in such and such a place there is a very huge tree. In such and such a forest there is a green tree, very- tall and broad, and even’ branch of it is big.” The king's envoy s who had braced his belt for the quest* was hearing a different kind of report from every one; So he travelled there for years, (whilst) the king kept sending money to him. After he had suffered much fatigue in that foreign land* at ifljs last he became too exhausted to seek (any longer). No trace of the object of pursuit was discovered: of what he W'anted nothing appeared but the report. The thread of his hope snapped f the thing he had sought became unsought m the end. He resolved to return to the king* (and set out) shedding tears and traversing the way. 1 Ijc* they enjoy spiritual power and freedom. 1 Literal fy, '"eats and takes." MATKNAWf, BOOK II How the Shaykh explained the hidden meaning of the free to the seeker who mw in the bondage of formalism. I here was a wise Shaykh s a noble Qufcb p at the halting-place where the king's intimate fell into despair. He (the envoy) said, “Being without hope, I will go to him, and set out on the road (again) from his threshold + In order that his prayer (blessing) may accompany me, since 1 have no hope of (winning) my heart's desire/" With tearful eyes he went to the Shaykh" he was raining tears, [ike a cloud, O Shaykh/' he cried, “it is the time for mercy and pity; 1 am in despair: now is the time for kindness.” He (the Shaykh) said, “Say plainly what is the cause of thy despair: what is thy object? what hast thou in view 1 ? 11 s®* 5 answered, “The Emperor chose me out to seek a certain branching tree, For there is a tree, unique in (all) the quarters (of the world): its fruit is (of) the substance pf the Water of Life. I have sought (it) for yearta and seen no sign (of il) except the gibes and ridicule of these merry men r ” I he Shaykh laughed and said to him, “Q simpleton, this is the tree of knowledge in the sage — Very high and very grand and very far-spreading: (it is} a ater ui Life from the all-encompassing Sea (of God). 3&7G Thou hast gone aiter the form, thou hast gone astray: thou eanst not find (it) because thou hast abandoned the reality. Sometimes it is named tree, sometimes sometimes it ]S named "sea,/ sometimes 'cloud/ (It is) that one (thing) from w hich a hundred thousand effects arise: its least effects are everlasting life. Although (in essence) it is single, it hath a thousand effects: mniimerablc names bent (may be properly applied to) that one (thing). One person may be father in relation to thee; in regard to another individual he may be son, .><<,£ In regard to another he may be wrath and a foe; in regard to another he may be graciousness and a friend. (He hath) hundreds of thousands of names, (but) he is one man: the owner of every quality belonging to him is blind to (incapable of) giving any (true) description (of him). Whoever seeks the (mere) name, if he is entrusted (with a confidential mission) he is hopeless and in distraction, even as thou art. Why dost thou stick to the name ‘ tree, 1 so that thou art left bitterly disappointed and ill-fortuned? 1 Literally, “towards what is thy face (turned)?" THE TREE OF LIFE +13 Pass on from the name and look at the attributes, in order that the attributes may show thee the way to the essence/' The disagreement of mankind is caused by names ; peace jsso ensues when they advance to the reality (denoted by the name). How four person* quarrelled about grapes, which were known to each of them by a different name. A certain man gave a dirhem to four persons: one of them (a Persian) said, "I will spend this on augur/* The second one was an Arab: he said, + No, I want 'inab, not angur+ O rascal I wt The third was a Turk; and he said, "This (money) is mine: I don't want 'ittab, 1 want uzum” The fourth, a Greek, said, 11 Stop this talk: I want istdftl/* These people began fighting in contention with one another, jse* because they were unaware of the hidden meaning of the names. In their folly they smote each other with their fists: they were full of ignorance and empty of knowledge. If a master of the esoteric had been there, a revered and many- languages! man, he would have pacified them; And then he would have said, u With this one dirhem 1 will give all of you what ye wish. When without deceit ye surrender your hearts (to me), this dirhem will do all this for you* Your one dirhem will become four 1 —the result desired: 1690 four enemies will become one through unanimity 2 . What each one of you says produces strife and separation; what I say brings you agreement. Therefore he ye mute T keep silence, that I may be your tongue in speech and talk." (Even) if in ihcir agreement with each other your words are (as) a strong rope, in effect they are a source of contention and distraction + Borrowed (accidental) heat produces no (essential) effect; natural heat hath (its own) virtue. If vou have made vinegar hot by means of fire, (still) when ^5 you drink it, it will undoubtedly increase the coldness (of your constitution), Because that (artificially produced) heat of it is exotic 3 : its fundamental nature is coldness and tartness. And (on the other hand)* though grape-syrup be frozen, my son* it will add heat to the liver when you drink it. The immature and the full-grown grape are opponents* but when the immature grape has ripened, it becomes a good friend. The immature grape that has remained stone-hard and crude — God in eternity has called it an original unbeliever* l ie (such a one) is neither a brother nor one (in) soul (with 172& the faithful Moslems): he is an ill-starred heretic in (the state of) damnation. If I should tell that which he keeps hidden (in his heart), there would arise in the world a sore temptation of (men's) minds, s Tis better that the secret of the blind infidel should be untold: 'tis better that the smoke of Hell should be banished from Tram. The speeches of princely birds 1 are (meaningless as) an echo; where is the speech of the birds of Solomon? Anas b. Malik said :The Messenger of Allah (May peace be upon him) used to come to visit us. I had a younger brother who was called Abu ‘Umair by Kunyah (surname). He had a sparrow with which he played, but it died. So one day the prophet (May peace be upon him) came to see him and saw him grieved. He asked: What is the matter with him? The people replied: His sparrow has died. He then said: Abu ‘Umair! What has happened to the little sparrow?

‘Abd al-Rahman b. ‘Abd Allah quoted his father as saying :When we were on a journey with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he had gone to releive himself, we saw a Hummarah with two young ones. We took the young ones. The Hummarah came and began to spread out its wings. Then the prophet (May peace be upon him) came and said : who has pained this young by the loss of her young? Give her young ones back to her. We also saw an ant-hill which we had burned. He asked? Who has burned this? We replied : we have. He said: it is not fitting that anyone but the lord of the fire should punish with fire

dense_mmr.text: THE MERCHANT AND THE PARROT IIozc the parrot bade farewell to the mm hunt and flew away. The parrot gave him one or two counsels full of (spiritual) ityj savour and after that bade him the farewell of parting. The merchant said to her, u Go f God protect thee! Just now thou hast shown to me a new Wav*" Said the merchant to himself, “This is the counsel for me; I will take her Way, for this Wav is shining with light. How should my soul be meaner than the parrot? The soul ought to follow a good track like this,” The harmfulness of being honoured by the people and of becoming conspicuous. The body is cage-like - the body, amidst the cajoleries of those who come in and go out, became a thorn to the soul. This one says to him, "l will be thy confidant,” and that 1850 one says, “ Nay, 1 am thy partner.” This one says to him, "There is none in existence like thee for beauty ancl eminence and for kindness and liberality.” That one says to him, "Both the worlds are thine* all our souls are thy soul's parasites/* When he sees the people intoxicated with (desire for) him, because of arrogance he loses self-control. He does not know that the Devil has cast thousands like him into the water of the river (of destruction)* The world's flattery and hypocrisy is a sweet morsel; cat less iSg* of it (eat it not), for it is a morsel full of fire. Its fire is hidden and its taste is manifest; its smoke becomes visible in the end. Do not say* "How should I swallow that praise? He is speaking from desire (for reward): I am on his track (and see quite well what he is after)/ 1 If your bdauder should satirise you in public, your heart would burn for (many) days on account of those scorches (of vituperation). Although you know that he (only) said it in disappointment because the hopes he had of you brought him no gairi h (Vet) the effect thereof is remaining within you. The same j&fo experience happens to you in the case of praise. The effect of that too lasts fur many days and becomes a source of arrogance and deception of the soul* But it does not $how r it$df> because praise is sweet; (in the case of blame) the evil shows itself, because blame is bitter* It (blame) is like (bitter) decoctions and pills which you swallow- and for a long time you arc in disturbance and pain, MATHNAWf, BOOK I Whereas s if you eat halted (sweetmeat) p its taste is momentary: this effect, like the other, is not end urine for ever. Since it does not endure (perceptibly), it endures imper¬ ceptibly: recognise every opposite by means of its opposite. When the effect of sugar endures (remains latent), after a while it produces boils that call for the lancet. Pharaoh was made (what he was) by abundance of praises; be lowly of spirit through meekness, do not domineer. So far as you can* become a slave, do not be a monarch. Suffer blows: become like the ball, do not be the bat. Otherwise, when this elegance and beauty remains with you no more, you will be loathed by those companions. iSjt? The set of people who used to flatter you deceitfully, when they behold you will call you a devil. When they see you at their doors, they all will cry, “A dead man has risen from his grave. M (You will be) like the beardless youth whom diey address as lb Lord vt that by this hypocrisy they may make him infamous. As soon as he has grown a beard in infamy, the Devil is ashamed to search after him. The Devil approaches Man for the sake of wickedness : he does not approach you because you are worse than the Devil* So long as you were a man the Devil was running at your heels and bidding you taste (his) wine. Since you have become confirmed in devilry, the Devil is fleeing from you, O good-for-nothing! At that (former) time they clung to your skirt: when you became like this they all fled. Explanation of {the Tradition) “ Whatsoever God trills tomttA to pass" We have spoken all these words, but in preparing ourselves (for the journey before us) we are naught, naught without the favours of God. Without the favours of God and God + s elect ones, angel though he be, his page is black. iwv O God, O Thou whose bounty fulfils (every') need, it is not allowable to mention any one beside Thee. This amount of guidance Thou hast bestowed (upon us); till this (present time) Thou hast covered up many a fault of ours. Cause the drop of knowledge which Thou gavest (us) hereto¬ fore to become united with Thy seas- In my soul there is a drop - of knowledge: deliver it from sensuality and from the body's clay, Before these clays drink it up, before these winds sweep it sway. THE ALM1GHTINES5 OF GOD JOJ Although, when they sweep it away. Thou art able to take it is^s back from them and redeem it. The drop that vanished in the air or was spilled (on the earth}—when did it flee {escape} from the storehouse of Thy omnipotence? If it enter into non-existence or a hundred non-existences, it will make a foot of its head (will return in headlong haste) when * Thou cal lest it. Hundreds of thousands of opposites are killing their oppo¬ sites: Thy decree is drawing them forth again {from non- existence) * There is caravan on caravan, O Lord, (speeding) continually from non-existence towards existence. In particular, every night all thoughts and understandings become naught, plunged in the deep Sea; Again at the time of dawn those Divine ones lift up their heads from the Sea, like fishes. In autumn the myriads of boughs and leaves go in rout into the sea of Death, (While) in the garden the crow clothed in black like a mourner makes lament over the (withered) greenery. ' , Again from the Lord of the land 1 comes the edict (saying) to Non-existence, “ Give back what thou hast devoured! Give up, O blaek Death, what thou hast devoured of plants 1*05 and heating herbs and leaves and grass!" O brother, collect thy wits for an instant (and think}: from moment to moment (incessantly) there is autumn and spring within thee. Behold the garden of die heart, green and moist ami fresh, full of rosebuds and cypresses and jasmines; Boughs hidden by the multitude jof leaves, vast plain and high palace hidden bv the multitude of flowers. These words, which are from Universal Reason, are the scent of those flowers and cypresses and hvacinths. Didst thou (ever) smell the Scent of a rose where no rose was? 1 *> Didst thou (ever) see the foaming of wine where no wine was? The scent is thy guide and conducts thee on thy way: it will bring thee to Eden and Kawthar, _ The scent is a remedy for the (sightless) eye; (it is) light¬ making: the eve of Jacob was opened by a scent. The foul scent darkens the eye, the scent of Joseph succours Tllou who art not a Joseph, be a Jacob: be (familiar), like him, with weeping and sore distress. Hearken to this counsel from the hageof Ghazna \ that thou j mayst feel Freshness in thy old body: 1 Literally ; "the headman of the village." 1 Sanri- t°4 MATHNAWf* BOOK I “Disdain needs a face like the rose; when thou hast not (such a face), do not indulge in 1 ill-temper. Ugly is disdain in an uncomely face, grievous is eye-ache in an unseeing eye / 1 In the presence of Joseph do not give thyself airs and behave like a beauty: offer nothing but the supplication and sighs of Jacob. The meaning of dying (as conveyed) by the parrot was supplication (self-abasement): make thyself dead in supplication and poverty (of spirit), wo That the breath of Jesus may revive thee and make thee fair and blessed as itself* How should a rock be covered with verdure by the Spring? Become earth, that thou may at grow flowers of many a hue. Years hast thou been a heart-jagging rock: once, for the sake of experiment, be earth! The story 0/ the old harper who in the time of 1 Umar, may God be well-pleased with him , on a day when he teas starving played the harp for God's sake in the graveyard. Hast thou heard that in the time of 'Umar there was a harper, a fine and glorious minstrel? The nightingale would be made beside herself by his voice: by his beautiful voice one rapture would be turned into a hundred. His breath was an ornament to assembly and congregation, and at his song the dead would arise. (He was) like Israfil (Seraphicl), whose voice will cunningly bring the souls of the dead into their bodies. Or he was (like) an accompanist z to Israfil, for his music would make the elephant grow tvings* One day l&rAfil will make a shrill sound and will give life to him that has been rotten for a hundred years. The prophets also have (spiritual) notes within, whence there comes life beyond price to them that seek (God) P The sensual ear does not hear those notes, for the sensual ear is defiled by iniquities. The note of the peri 3 is not heard by man t for he is unable to apprehend the mysteries of the peris, Although the note of the peri too belongs to this world. The note of the heart is higher than both breaths (notes) 4 . For peri and man (alike) are prisoners: bom are (captive) in the prison of this ignorance. THE STORY OF THE HARPER 105 Recite Q community of Jinn (and mm) in the Siiratu P- Rahman; recognise (the meaning of) j f ye be abie to pass forth , The inward notes of the saints say, at first, il O ye particles i-)=s of Id (not = Hot-being), Take heed, lift up your heads from the Id of negation, put forth your heads from this fancy and vain imagining. 0 ye who all are rotten m (the world of) generation and cor¬ ruption, vour everlasting soul neither grew nor came to birth/' If I tell (even) a tittle of those (saintly) notes, the souls will lift up their heads from the tombs. Put thine ear close, for that (melody) is not far off, but T ri$ not permitted to convey it to thee. Hark! for the saints are the Iariffla of the (present) time: from them to the dead comes Life and freshness. At their voice the dead souls in the body's grave start up in their winding-sheets. He (that is thus awakened) says, “This voice is separate from (all other) voices: to quicken (the dead) is the work of the voice of God. We (had) died and were entirely decayed: the call of God ca me: we all arose/’ The call of God, (whether it be) veiled or unveiled, bestows that which He bestowed on Mary from fils bosom. 0 ye who are rotten with death (in your hearts) underneath 1935 the skin, return from non-existence at the voice of the Friend! Absolutely, indeed, that voice is from the King (God), though it be from the larynx of God's sen-ant. He (God) lias said to him (the saint), “I am thy tongue and eye; I am thy senses and l am thy good pleasure and thy wrath. Go, for thou art (he of whom God saith), 1 By Me he hears and by Me he sees 1 : thou art the (Divine) consciousness (itself): what is the occasion (propriety') of (saying), 'Thou art the possessor of the (Divine) consciousness'? Since thou hast become p through bewilderment, * He that belongs to God/ I am thine* for s God shall belong to him/ Sometimes 1 say to thee, “Tis thou/ sometimes, 'Tis I 1 : f-j+u whatever I say, I am the Sun illuminating (all). Wheresoever 1 shine forth from the lamp-niche of a breath (Divine word), there the difficulties of a (whole) world are resolved. The darkness which the (earthly) sun did not remove, through My breath that darkness becomes like bright morning/' To an Adam He In His own person showed the (Divine) Names; to the rest He was revealing the Names by means of Adam. Do thou receive His light either from Adam or from Himself: take the wine either from the jar or from the gourd (cup), io6 MATHNAWf, BOOK ] For this gourd is very dowdy connected with the jar: the blessed gourd is not rejoiced (by the same causes) as thou art. Mustafa (Mohammed) said, “Happy he that has seen me and he that looks at him that saw my face,” When a lamp has derived (its) light from a candle, every one that sees it (the lamp) certainly sees the candle. If transmission (of the light) occurs in this way till a hundred lamps (are lighted), the seeing of the last (lamp) hecumes a meeting with the original (light) 1 . Either take with (all) thy soul from the hindmost light — there is no difference—or from the candelabrum. t s SQ Either behold the light (of God) from the lamp of the last (saints), or behold His light from the candle of those who have gone before. Explanation of the Tradition , " Verify, your Lord hath, during the days of your time , certain breathings: oh, address your- selves to {receive} them.” The Prophet said, “In these days the breathings of God prevail : Keep ear and mind (attentive) to these (spiritual) influences, catch up such-like breathings. 1 ’' The (Divine) breathing came, beheld you, and departed: it gave life to whom It would, and departed. Another breathing has arrived. Be thou heedful, that thou mavst not miss this one too, O comrade, i,., i55 The soul of fire gained therefrom an extinguisher of (its) fire, the dead soul felt within itself a movement (of life). This is the freshness and movement of the Tubd-tree, this is not like the movements of animals. If it fait on earth and heaven, their galls will turn to water at once (they will be consumed with terror). Truly, from fear of this infinite breath (they were filled with dismay): recite (the words of the Qur’an) but they reftised to bear it (the trust offered to them). Else, how should (the words) they shrank from it have been (in the Qur’dn), unless from fear of it the heart of the mountain had become blood? 1560 Yesternight this (breath) presented itself (to me) in a different guise (but) some morsels (of food) came in and barred the way. To slay this (enemy) is not the work of reason and intelli¬ gence: the inward lion is not subdued by the hare. u ?3 This carnal self (nafi) is Hell, and Hell is a dragon (the fire of) which is not diminished by oceans (of water). To Noah his people said, 1 Where is the Divine recompense? * He said, 'On the other side of they cover themselves with their garments „ Ye have wrapped your faces and heads in your clothes: of mg* necessity ye have eyes and see not,' Man is eye, and (all) the rest is (worthless) skin: the sight of that (eye) is (consists in) seeing the Beloved. When there is not sight of the Beloved, it (the eye) is better blind; the beloved who b not everlasting is better afar (away and out of sight),” When the ambassador of Rfint admitted these fresh (spiritual) words into his hearing (gave ear to them), be became more full of longing. MATHNAWf, BOOK I He fixed his eye on seeking ‘Umar, he let hi$ baggage and horse be lost. 1410 He was going in every direction after that man of (great) accomplishment, inquiring madly for him, Saying, “Can there be in the world such a man, and he be hid, like the spirit, from the world? ” He sought him, that he might be as a slave to him: inevitably the seeker is a finder. An Arab woman of the desert saw that he was a stranger- guest. “Look,” said she, “there is ‘Umar under that palm. There he is under the palm-tree, apart from the people: behold the Shadow of God asleep in the shade!*' How the ambassador of Rum found the Commander of the Faithful, * Umar, may God be toell-pleased faith him, sleeping tinder the palm-tree. 1413 He came thither and stood afar off; he saw ‘Umar and fell a-trembling. An awe came upon the ambassador from that slumbering man; a sweet ecstasy lodged in his soul. Love and awe are contrary to each other; he saw these two contraries united in his heart 1 . He said to himself : “ I have seen (many) kings, I have been great (in esteem) and chosen (for honour) in the presence of sultans: I had no awe or dread of kings, (but) awe of this man has robbed me of my wits, t4 «■ I have gone into a jungle of lions and leopards, and my face did not change colour because of them; Often where the ranks are arrayed on the field of battle have I become (fierce) as a lion at the time when the affair is grievous (desperate) ; Many a heavy blow have I suffered and inflicted, I have been stouter in heart than (all) the others. This man is asleep on the earth, unarmed, (and yet) I am trembling in my seven limbs (my whole body): what is this? This is awe of God, it is not from created beings, it is not awe of this man who wears the frock of a dervish. i^ij Whoever is afraid of God and has chosen fear of God (as his religion), the jinn and mankind and every one who sees (him) are afraid of him.” Thus meditating, he folded his hands reverently. After a while 'Umar sprang up from sleep. 1 Literally , 11 liver.' 4 UMAR AND THE AMBASSADOR How the ambassador of Rum saluted the Commander of the Faithful t may God be ell-pleased with him. The unveiling is witnessed by the king and by others as well* (but) at the time of being alone (with the bride) there is no one except the mighty king. The bride unveils before commons and nobles (alike); in the bridal chamber the king is (alone) with the bride. He ('Umar) reminded him of the stages traversed by the suul s and he reminded him of the journeys of the spirit. And of the Time which has (ever) been void of time, and of i-uo the Station of Holiness which has (ever) been majestical* And of the atmosphere wherein the Simurgh of the spirit h before this (material life), has flown and experienced (the bounty of Divine) grace 1 . Every single flight thereof (being) greater than the horizons (of this world) and greater than the hope and greed of the longing lover. dense_mmr.text: THE DEAK MAN AND THE INVALID THE DEAK MAN AND THE INVALID iSj If you become an exponent (imitator) of the song of birds, how will you become acquainted with the (real) meaning of the bird? , , , If you learn the note of a nightingale, how will you know what '(feelings) it has towards a rose? t Or if vou do know, ’twill be tram analogy and surmise, like the conjectures formed by deaf people from those who move their lips. Haiti the deaf mart went to visit his sick neighbour. One possessed of much wealth said to a deaf man, A jjf* neighbour of thine is fallen ill. . The deaf man said to himself, “Being hard of hearing, what shall I understand of the words spoken by that youth?— Especially (as) he is ill and his voice is weak; but I must go thither, there's no escape. When l sec his lips moving, I will form a conjecture as to that (movement) from myself. When 1 say, ‘ How are you, O my suffering (fnend)? he will replv,' 1 am fine ’ or ‘ I am pretty well.* I will say, ‘Thanks (to God)! What posset have you had to 3 J r , 5 drink? * He will reply, ‘ Some sherbet ’ or * a decoction of kidney- beans. P ‘ (Then) I will say,' May you enjoy health! Who is the doctor attending you?’ He will answer, ‘So-and-so. Tie is one who brings great luck with him 1 , I will remark; * since he has come, things will go well for you. I have experienced (the luck of) his foot: wherever he goes, the desired object is attained.’ ” The good man made ready these conjectural answers, and went to see the invalid. „ “How are you?" he asked, "1 am at the point oi death, said he. " Thanks (to God)l" cried the deaf man. At this, the patient became resentful and indignant, ... , ,. , Saving (to himaelf), “What (cause for) thanksgiving is this? He has been my enemy.”—The deaf man made a conjecture, and (as now appears) it has turned out to be wrong. After that, he asked him what he had drunk, ‘‘ Poison, sake he. “May it do you good and give you health!” said the deaf man. His (the invalid^) wrath increased. . Then he inquired, “ Which of the doctors is it that is coming to attend vou?” . „ , . ^ He replied, “Aaracl (the Angel of Death) is coming, .id you gone!” ‘‘His foot (arrival),” said the deaf man, “is very blessed: be glad! ” l Literally, "one whose foot is very blest.*’ 1S4 MATHNAWf f BOOK I The deaf man went forth. He add gaily, "Thanks (to God) fur that! Kow r I will take leave/* The invalid said^ "This is my mortal foe: I did not know he was (such) a mine of iniquity/' The mind of the invalid was seeking a hundred abusive terms, that he might send him a message (filled with abuse) of every description , As, when any one has eaten bad (indigestible) food, it is turning his heart (stomach) until he vomits. Suppression of anger is (like) this: do not vomit it, so that you may gain sweet words in recompense. Since he had no patience, he was tormented. "Where.” he cried, "is this cur, mis infamous cuckold p That 1 may pour upon him tvhat he said (make a retort in his own style)?—far at that time the Hon of my thought was asleep (l was too weak to contend with him). Inasmuch as visiting the sick is for the purpose of (giving them) tranquillity, this is not a visit to the sick: it is the satis¬ faction of an enemywt$h. (His motive was) that he should see his enemy enfeebled and that his wicked heart should be at peace.” Many are they that do works of devotion and set their hearts on being approved and rewarded for the same. 3 'Ti$ in truth a lurking sin: that which he (the pietist) thinks pure is (really) foul. As (in the case of) the deaf man, who fancied that he did a kindness, but it had the opposite result. He sits down well-pleased, saying, " 1 have paid my respects, I have performed what was due'to my neighbour"; (But) lie has (only) kindled a fire (of resentment) against himself in the invalid’s heart and burned himself. Beware, then, of the fire that ye have kindled: verily ye have increased in sin. r ^ The Prophet said to our desert Arab, "Pray 1 , for indeed thou hast not prayed (aright), my man.” As a means of preventing these dangers, uj m comes - in every (ritual) prayer, lliat is to say, "O God, do not mingle my prayer w r ith the prayer of the erring and the hypocrites.” By the analogical reasoning which the deaf man adopted a ten years' friendship was made vain. Especially, Q master, (you must avoid) the analogy drawn by the low senses in regard to the Revelation which is ilEimitable. ;9 5 If your sensuous ear is fit for (understanding) the letter (of the Revelation), know that your ear that receives the occult 2 (meaning) is deaf. 1 /j. 11 perform the rituil prayer,” 3 Head

dense_mmr.text: THE KING AND THE HANDMAIDEN THE KING AND THE HANDMAIDEN It Since his name has come (to my lips), it behaves me to set forth some hint of his bounty. At this moment my Soul 1 has plucked my skirt: he has caught i : the perfume of Joseph's vest, (He said): “For the sake of our years of companionship, recount one of those sweet ecstasies. That earth and heaven may laugh (with joy), that intellect and spirit and eye may increase a hundredfold/* (I said): "Du not lay tasks on me, for ] have passed away from myself [fand)\ iny apprehensions are blunted and I know not how to praise. Everything that is said by one who has not returned to con¬ sciousness, if he constrains himself or boastfully exaggerates, is unseemly. How should I — not a vein of mine is sensible — describe that i .■> Friend who hath no peer? The description of this severance and this heart's blood do chou at present leave over till another time/' He said: “Feed me, for I am hungry, and make haste, for Time is a cutting sword. The Sufi is the son of the (present) timc% Q comrade: it ts not the rule of die Way to sav ‘To-morrow/ Art not thou indeed a Sufi, then? That which is (in hand) is reduced to naught by postponing the payment,” I said to him: “It is better that the secret of die Friend should i :s be disguised: do thou hearken (to it as implied) in the contents of the tale. It is better that the lovers' secret should be told in the talk of others.'* He said: “Tell it forth openly and nakedly and without un¬ faithfulness: do not put me off, O trifler! Lift the veil and speak nakedly, for 1 ! do not wear a shirt when I sleep with the Adored One/ 1 I said: 11 If Fie should become naked in (thy) vision, neither wilt thou remain nor thy bosom nor thy waist. Ask thy wish, but a$k with measure: a blade of straw will not support the mountain* It the Sun, by whom this world is illumined, should approach a little (nearer), all will be burned. Do not seek trouble and turmoil and bloodshed: say no more concerning the .Sun of Tabriz! pp This (mystery) hath no end: tell of the beginning. Go, relate the conclusion of this tale, * tJusarniTddfn.
